#5787. These Are The Stories Of The First Time The Jalopnik Audience Drove A Car

Earlier this week we asked you to take a trip down memory lane and share the story of your very first time driving a car, and it seems like a lot of you have really great dads, since most of you said you first drove on your dad's lap as a kid. Beyond the lap driving though, you, the dear, sweet Jalopnik audience, shared lots of entertaining memories. This is only a roundup of a few popular answers, but feel free to go back and read through the ones that didn't make the cut.

I recounted the story of the first time I took the keys to a friend's second-generation Nissan Altima and invited myself to do some acceleration runs in a parking lot when I was in middle school, which is a bad idea and is absolutely not something that anyone else should do, to be clear. We're not glorifying car theft, underage, or unlicensed driving here, we're just sharing some stories. If you have an exceptionally entertaining tale, feel free to share it in the comments section below, but these are a few of the stories behind the Jalopnik audience's first time driving a car.

The first time i drove a car, my dad had terminal cancer, and i was 14 years old. In our huge Dallas neighborhood, he would pretend to pass out and tell me to take the wheel of the 1999 Plymouth Grand Voyager!

A few weeks later on a Saturday or Sunday he took me to an empty elementary school parking lot, and taught me how finally use the steering wheel while being in the correct seat and how to get used to the pedals.

My by the book father, broke the rules to teach me skill he knew i was itching to learn. One of the most fun weekends of my life. He made it another 8 months, and took me out to different parking lots on weekends that he was feeling well! Made that time a little bit easier on both of us i think.

The day of my 16th birthday, my mom drove me to the DMV to get my learner's permit. As we walked out to the car, me with my fresh permit in my hand, it was snowing like a banshee. My mom handed me the keys and said, "You get to drive us home."

We lived on a hill, and as I tried to slow down and turn into our driveway, (no ABS or stability control back in the '80s) I ended up sliding into the neighbor's front yard and taking out her wooden flower boxes.

For the next couple of months it was a very snowy winter, so I learned how to become a great driver on snow and ice. I took my driver's test in February during a snowstorm and passed it on the first try.

Until the day I got my learner's permit, I had never driven a car before.

I grew in dairy farm in rular Finland, so I've been operating heavy equipment since I was heavy enough to press clutch and brakes. So around 6 years old back in the golden 80's. My first run with car was our Saab 99 around 7 years old. It was first gasoline powered vehicle I've tested, so throttle surprised me a bit and I ran over our laundry drying apparatus. Father was not pleased. However first proper drive was around 10-11 year old, when my grandfather had accident with tractor PTO and lost his thumb. It was bleeding quite a lot so I drove him 5km to health center. Nobody batted eyelid to that :D.

First time I drove solo was to go from home to my parent's florist. Easy drive. Had to turn right on a busy road that had about 6 lanes. I had a green light and just took it. Didn't realize that someone was taking a left coming the other way and going into my lane. I had to brake hard to avoid hitting them. Then they brake checked and cut me off a couple times as I tried to drive safely and easily. Eventually, they got mad at someone else and intentionally caused an accident. Today we call that Road Rage. I had no concept of what it was and how it worked and was scared to death.

I grew up on a small farm, so I drove our vehicles around some well before I had my permit. But my dad would take my brother and me to the Eagle River area in Wisconsin every summer, and one time he took us to dinner and afterwards realized he was not fit to drive. So he had me drive the three of us back to the cabin. I was 14. He said I did a good job, but how would he know? 😂

I remember he had a black third-gen Nissan Maxima. But I'm sure I drove so carefully and slowly it didn't matter what it was.

For me, it was easy: Dad was the local Chevrolet dealer up until about eight months before my sixteenth birthday. He'd had a long habit of bringing home whatever was the strangest car in the used lot when he came home for lunch, so I could spend the hour crawling all over it. We had a very long driveway, and lived at the end of a three block long dead end street. So, by the time I'd turned twelve, if the car had an automatic I'd invariably get behind the wheel, first laps in the driveway, and shortly after six block long round trips. The first car was a Renault Dauphine with push-button automatic transmission.

More on the lines of what you're looking for: The first 'illegal' drive was grabbing dad's company car (1965 Impala SS hardtop) and taking it for a 15-20 mile drive in the summer of 1965 while the rest of the family was on the weekly summer drive in Mom's station wagon. Shortly thereafter, realizing he was leaving the dealership (I didn't know) dad swapped the Impala for a Corvair Monza coupe because his kid was a complete Corvair junkie. Had it out a couple of times, too.

My father was an incredibly strict disciplinarian (egged on my mom, who was the real force) except when it came to cars. I got away with murder on that, and I'm certain I wasn't getting away with nearly as much as I thought I did at the time.

I was 13. My (unknown to me at the time) doper uncle asked me, "Have you ever driven a car?" He fixed my reply by letting me drive him around Alabama backroads for an hour in his MGB. I was so excited later that afternoon to tell my parents what John let me do. They did not share my excitement.

As for me, I got a lifetime love of cars, especially rowing my own. RIP, Uncle John!

I used to live in farm country, we weren't farmers, but fields for miles in the Salinas Valley. I was 12 or 13 when my father took me to a dirt lot out in the fields. There he turned me loose in a 1972 VW squareback. With in 5 – 10 minutes I was cruising around that lot like I had been driving my whole life. Also most will admit that early air cooled VWs are extremely forgiving, and easy to drive. When done in the dirt lot he told me to go ahead and drive home. Taught me the rules of the road, signs, don't run over people, etc. I was excited to say the least. The next morning he had me drive us from home to work, then school which was 20 miles on the 101 hwy. From that day on, I drove everyday to my father's shop. And he would always tell me "straight to school, and back." Like I listened.

#5786. The EV Takeover Is Taking Shape, Despite Heroic Efforts To Stop It

Whelp, the AI boom has had one positive knock-on effect. It is creating new multi-millionaires by the bushel, any one of whom can afford to splurge on a pricey new electric vehicle. That aside, EV stakeholders in the US are springing back to life after a year-long slumber. Even General Motors is in play, stirring up long lost memories of its 1990’s-era EV1 debacle instead of hiding its head in shame. What’s up with that?

I’m just going to stick my neck out and say that the eponymous Aptera solar-powered autocycle from the US startup Aptera will attract enough AI-enriched drivers to make a go of it. The on-again, off-again, on-again automaker has been on this year, working towards volume production of a plug-in, three-wheeled two-seater EV that can travel up to 40 miles on its own solar-plus-storage system (see more Aptera news here).

Autocycles were once common here in the US and overseas markets, distinguished from motorcycles by their front-facing seats and steering wheels, rather than straddled seats and handlebars. They fell out of favor in the US by the middle of the 20th century, but 21st century hot-rodders have revived the form with a focus on eyebrow-raising, open-air, gas-guzzling showpieces. In particular, interest has spread in states that do not require autocycle drivers to invest in an additional motorcycle license.

The Aptera is showy in its own right, resembling a rocket ship with unique aerodynamic styling. Perhaps it may even show up in the next James Bond adventure with James Pattinson at the wheel. In the meantime, the company has just made good on its pledge to reward early investors in the world’s first solar-powered car with the first production models to role off the assembly line. Aptera #1 goes to the founder and CEO of GDP Venture, Martin Hartono, aka “Accelerator #1.”

Drivers can reserve an Aptera of their own for just $100, and they can expect to pay about $40,000 for the ride. Considering that the solar fuel is free, anyone in the mood for a head-turning ride will get quite a bargain for their $40,000 compared to other competitors in the zero emission two-seater field, such as the recently refreshed Tesla Roadster.

Speaking of refresh, General Motors has been weirdly lavishing attention on the EV1 sedan all this year, even though the automaker has been roundly criticized for the killing the short-lived car in its cradle. The automaker began producing EV1 electric sedans starting in 1996, following the unveiling of its Impact electric concept car in 1990. Unlike the Impact, EV1 was designed for use on the road. However, it was also designed mainly for the California market, and primarily for lease, not for sale. Production halted in 2003 at just about 1,000 vehicles, all to be recalled by GM and sent to the crusher as chronicled in Chris Paine’s 2006 documentary, “Who Killed The Electric Car?”

Or, maybe not so weird after all. GM’s electrification journey long predates the launch of Tesla Motors in 2003. The legacy automaker is now determined to stake out its claim on automotive history, with 2026 marking the 30th anniversary of the start of EV1 production.

GM has been celebrating the anniversary all this year with multiple long form articles about the Impact and EV1 on its website, eager to remind everybody that its industry-leading vehicle electrification efforts of the 1990’s continue to manifest decades later, in the form of heat pumps for climate control, by-wire technology, and regenerative braking among other elements.

GM’s latest love letter to the EV1 popped up on November 17, when the automaker officially celebrated the completed restoration of the EV1 “V212” alongside its a private owner, Billy Caruso. The rare survivor of GM’s the junkyard crusher was evidently hiding out in an impound lot in Georgia all these years, until Caruso acquired it at auction and enlisted Jared Pink of the popular show The Questionable Garage to fix it up. Considering TQG’s large following on YouTube, GM wisely lent its engineers to the effort, along with several donated parts from its own EV1.

US President Donald Trump and the Republican majority in Congress have made a heroic effort to dial down the vehicle electrification movement, but facts on the ground keep getting in their way. For starters, today’s advanced batteries apply across multiple energy resources, fossil and non-fossil alike. So, it’s no surprise to see the US Department of Energy continuing to throw taxpayer dollars at new energy storage projects (here’s one example), even though some of that activity will eventually ripple into the vehicle electrification field.

The US Department of Defense is also getting into the act. DoD’s electrification journey has been a tedious one, but in recent years it has begun creeping stealthily towards a vision of ground mobility enabled by electricity, providing the key tactical advantages of silent running and a low heat signature.

The latest news on that score involves a $1.4 billion loan commitment from DoD’s Office of Strategic Capital (OSC), enabling the silicon-based battery materials startup Sila to vault its signature product into commercial production. DoD’s primary interest in the company consists of applications in the electric drone and autonomous mobility fields, but Sila has long been eyeballing the EV market as well.

Sila secured the loan commitment in August, and it has not let the grass grow under its feet. On November 18 the company announced an off-take agreement with the well-known Tesla EV battery supplier Panasonic Energy Corporation of North America. “The multi-year agreement is part of a long-term commercial relationship with the potential for over $1 billion of offtake over time,” Sila explained in a press statement, further elaborating that Panasonic will deploy its proprietary Titan Silicon silicon-carbon anode material in battery cells.

“The partnership is also expected to support significant manufacturing and construction job creation in the United States. With Sila’s U.S.-based anode production underpinned by proprietary American technology and know-how, Panasonic and its OEM customers gain a clearer path toward a more secure, resilient, and sustainable domestic supply chain,” Sila emphasized.

That’s…interesting! Aside from Tesla as one of Sila’s OEM customers, keep an eye on another Panasonic offtaker, the up-and-comer US startup Harbinger Motors, which also has a foot in the DoD door.

Photo: The vehicle electrification movement is far from over in the US, with the startup Aptera among the stakeholders betting on an EV sales rebound in the coming years (cropped, courtesy of Aptera).

#5785. Blood Test May Detect CTE During Life, Study Shows

— "This is a game changer," leading CTE researcher says

Detecting chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) in living patients may soon be possible, according to preliminary data from a case series.

CTE, a neurodegenerative disease associated with repetitive head impacts from contact sports, currently can be diagnosed only at autopsy.

In a study of 21 former American football players who had donated their brains, however, blood levels of endogenously cleaved microtubule-binding region tau (eMTBR-tau) were higher in CTE-positive participants than in CTE-negative participants (β=1.61, 95% CI 0.51-2.70), reported Annalise Miner, a PhD candidate working on research under Michael Alosco, PhD, of Boston University, at the Clinical Trials on Alzheimer's Disease conference in Boston.

Concentrations of eMTBR-tau were highest in former players who also had Alzheimer's pathology at autopsy. Levels were intermediate in those with high-stage CTE who did not have Alzheimer's pathology, Miner said.

Players with high-stage CTE had higher eMTBR-tau concentrations than those with low-stage or no CTE, she added. Blood levels of phosphorylated tau 217 (p-tau217) were negative or intermediate in CTE cases, except in athletes with comorbid Alzheimer's disease.

The study was published simultaneously in JAMA.

"This is a game changer," co-author Alosco said in a statement. "We are still in the discovery phase and it's a small sample size, but if future studies validate these findings, this blood test will allow us to detect CTE with a high level of accuracy and open the doors to clinical trials and treatment."

The findings mirrored those of a case-control study led by Washington University in St. Louis, which was presented at a scientific meeting in Japan last week and also published in JAMA. That study showed plasma eMTBR-tau243 was elevated in late-stage CTE and some other tauopathies.

Both eMTBR-tau and eMTBR-tau243 measure the same key biological features, Miner noted. "Recent findings demonstrate a strong correlation between the immunoassay-derived eMTBR-tau and the mass spectrometry-derived eMTBR-tau243, supporting the biological relevance of this immunoassay," she said.

CTE remains a major diagnostic challenge, noted Carla Palleis, MD, and Günter Höglinger, MD, both of LMU University Hospital in Munich. "A biomarker capable of identifying CTE-associated tau pathology could improve selection of appropriate participants for research studies, facilitate clinicopathological studies, and ultimately support the evaluation of preventive and therapeutic interventions," they wrote in a JAMA editorial.

Detecting CTE at an early stage could be particularly valuable when clinical features seem nonspecific, the editorialists pointed out. Distinguishing traumatic encephalopathy syndrome -- a clinical syndrome associated with CTE -- from other causes of cognitive or behavioral symptoms can be difficult.

"Future studies should determine whether eMTBR-tau improves the ability of the criteria for traumatic encephalopathy syndrome to distinguish it and identify individuals with underlying CTE neuropathology, particularly in the presence of Alzheimer's disease copathology," Palleis and Höglinger wrote.

Over several years, eMTBR has emerged as blood biomarker for Alzheimer's disease. A 2025 study showed that eMTBR-tau243 was more strongly associated with tau tangle pathology in Alzheimer's than other established blood biomarkers. More recent work showed that blood tests measuring p-tau217 and eMTBR-tau243 improved triage and reduced overdiagnosis in people with asymptomatic Alzheimer's pathology.

Of the 21 former American football players included in the new study, 12 played professionally, seven played in college, and two played at the high school level. Eighteen former players had an autopsy diagnosis of CTE; of these, 16 had high-stage CTE (stage III or IV) and two had low-stage CTE (stage I or II). Five CTE-positive participants had intermediate or high Alzheimer's disease neuropathology.

Most participants were white and were diagnosed with traumatic encephalopathy syndrome cognitive impairment, Miner noted.

This work represents a first step toward a CTE biomarker framework, she observed. "By combining plasma eMTBR tau with Alzheimer's biomarkers like p-tau217, we may be able to capture complementary information that helps us move closer to diagnosing CTE during life," Miner said.

#5784. MAGA-Loving Elon Musk Says He's 'Not MAGA,' Feels 'Foolish' Over Spending $445 Million On Dud Republican Midterm Election Campaigns

Good morning! It's Friday, November 20, 2026, and this is The Morning Shift, your daily roundup of the top automotive headlines from around the world, in one place. This is where you'll find the most important stories that are shaping the way Americans drive and get around.

In this morning's edition, Elon Musk knows he blew $500 million on the 2026 midterms, General Motors wants to double the money it makes off the war machine, Japan's largest automakers are banding together to standardize some processes and Mercedes-Benz says some German plants are in jeopardy as work stoppages spread.

If you'd like a recap of the latest auto news sent to your inbox each weekday, you can sign up for Jalopnik's free Morning Shift newsletter here.

It's no secret that Republicans across the U.S. went through an all-time drubbing during the midterm elections earlier this month, and while there were many losers, perhaps none was as big as Elon Musk. The Tesla CEO and Republican version of George Soros dropped over $445 million during the election cycle in a futile attempt to get his candidates into office. That very much didn't work, and now he has buyers remorse.

In truth, it's possible that the garish sums of money Elon spent on the election may have hurt the candidates he backed more than helped them, providing opponents with easy targets to latch onto. I mean, it's not hard to claim that the guy you're running against is back by Big Money when the world's richest man is bankrolling their campaign.

In any case, Elon really wishes he could turn back time, and he's about to have a hell of a lot more to answer for when it comes to his companies as emboldened Democratic leaders vow to investigate Trump and his buddies. From Bloomberg:

"I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seeing much for it," the billionaire said late Wednesday at the New York Times' DealBook Summit. "Probably, if I could rewind the clock, I would have spent less money."

Musk's political money overwhelmingly went to lost causes. Two super political action committees he funded — America PAC and Texas PAC — spent heavily to back Republican Senate and House candidates who lost, Federal Election Commission filings show. Ken Paxton's unsuccessful bid to win Texas' open Senate seat drew the lion's share of the money, at some $229 million.

Democrats also won major races further down the ballot in Texas, where Musk has built much of his corporate empire. Tesla has a sprawling factory near Austin, SpaceX launches rockets from its coastal hub reincorporated as Starbase, and the two companies plan to jointly build a chip factory called Terafab.

Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has taken issue with departing Governor Greg Abbott agreeing to award $1.7 billion in tax breaks for the Terafab project and singled out other state grants SpaceX has received. She called for an immediate moratorium on data center development during her campaign and accused developers of raising utility rates and depleting water supply.

Musk nevertheless downplayed the likelihood of any conflict with Hinojosa, saying he expects her to be "quite moderate."

"I don't think she's a far-left governor," he said. "Based on everything I've heard about her, I think things will be fine in Texas."

When asked about the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee telling Trump and unspecified corporate actors to lawyer up, Musk said some in the party were being "a little over the top."

During his appearance over a livestream from China, Musk sought to distance himself from the Make American Great Again movement, describing himself as ideologically moderate. "I'm not MAGA," he said.

Technically, Musk is correct. He's not MAGA. As he told supporters in 2024, he is actually "Dark MAGA."

General Motors wants to expand the money it makes off of wars by more than doubling its defense revenue to $2 billion in the next few years. It looks to take advantage of global defense companies turning to its automotive technology to accelerate their weapons production.

Back in August, GM delivered its first batch of Patriot missile components to Lockheed Martin within 22 days of the two companies entering a partnership in weapons manufacturing — something championed by the Trump administration. Several other large defense companies with governmental ties have also lined up to sign deals with GM. From the Financial Times:

"We have massive manufacturing capabilities to build defence equipment components. We have so many defence companies coming to us and saying help us," Stephen duMont, head of GM Defense, said in an interview in London.

In recent years, companies including Volkswagen, Jaguar Land Rover and Renault have diversified into the defence sector in search of new sources of revenue as profits become squeezed in the traditional automotive business due to cut-throat competition and higher costs.

Jim Farley, Ford's chief executive, confirmed earlier this year that it was also in discussions with the US government on defence-related projects, while Stellantis last week agreed to sell its Brampton plant to Canadian armoured vehicle maker Roshel and explore "global collaboration".

GM's ties to defence stretch back decades. It played a pivotal part in America's "Arsenal of Democracy" campaign during the second world war, converting all of its US plants to support the war effort. The group sold its defence business in 2003 and later re-established GM Defense as a subsidiary in 2017 after Mary Barra became chief executive.

"Mary recognised from early on the opportunity to leverage GM's investment in the automotive business for profitable growth of the defence business," said duMont, a former Raytheon executive.

The defence unit, a separate subsidiary that now has about 500 to 600 employees, was "like a start-up", allowing for quicker decision-making and operational changes.

In the grand scheme of things (read: General Motors), the defense unit is minuscule. It only generates about $1 billion in revenue every year, which isn't exactly nothing, but when compared with the group's total revenue of $185 billion, it's sort of small potatoes. That's why CEO Mary Barra wants to expand it.

It isn't just parts of weapons, either. It's also vehicles. The U.S. Army recently increased orders for Infantry Squad Vehicles from an initial 649 vehicles to nearly 12,000 — which could lead to a $1 billion contract. In addition, it's looking at getting in on the defense business in Europe and the UK.

The business of war is booming, and GM wants in on the action.

Japan's largest automakers, including Toyota, Honda and Nissan, are starting a new initiative to compete less and collaborate more as a way to deal with cheap Chinese competition. The first three things they'll do are harmonize quality criteria for steel, unify recycling protocols for plastics, and create a universal color-coding scheme for wire harnesses, but more steps are on the way. The Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association says these and any other big changes are coming to any suppliers doing business with Japanese automakers. From Automotive News:

Discussions will begin with Japanese suppliers but soon encompass international ones.

JAMA Chairman Koji Sato, who is also vice chairman of Toyota Motor Corp., launched the campaign after taking the helm of the industry lobby group in January. Leaders announced an agreement on steel, resin, and wire harnesses at the group's last regular meeting of the year here to set the stage for implementing harmonization from 2027.

The urgent efficiency drive is one of the most ambitious attempts yet to reshape a sprawling supply base spanning Toyota, Nissan, Honda, Mazda, Subaru, Mitsubishi and Suzuki. The goal: sharpen Japan Inc.'s edge amid an onslaught of new technologies and cutthroat new competitors from China by cutting costs and channeling the savings into innovation.

"We all share this strong sense of crisis, creating a momentum for change," Sato said. "Based upon our sense of a crisis, we decided to choose these three areas."

A JAMA task force leading the push has been working all year to formulate a framework. They decided on steel, resin and wire harnesses partly because they are areas of the vehicle that go unnoticed by customers and do not directly impact brand value or differentiation. The areas also account for a large portion of a vehicle's input costs, allowing for a large immediate impact.

JAMA said about 70,000 variants of wire harnesses are a prime candidate for consolidation.

Japan will consolidate and rationalize low-volume steel materials.

The group will standardize steel requirements that used to be specific to each carmaker and work to implement these new standards with the Japan Iron and Steel Federation.

Japan will standardize what kind of plastic and resin materials are recycled and how the materials are evaluated. This will help secure domestic sourcing through recycling.

Standardization will focus on sorting methods, traceability and design for easy disassembly.

Even beyond the idea of fending off Chinese competition, I think collaboration like this is a solid approach. If this type of shared componentry doesn't materially change the car, there's no real harm, and it cuts down on the supply chain waste of having every manufacturer have its own supply chain and specifications.

A senior labor leader in Germany is skeptical of Mercedes-Benz's plan to solve the company's problems by simply forcing staff to work longer hours — adding that the future of its plants would still be uncertain. Even a deal that would extend the 35-hour work week would leave underutilized factories and unresolved questions over the automaker's model lineup, according to IG Metall's Barbara Resch. From Bloomberg:

"We need a management board that believes in Germany as an industrial location — and demonstrates that with firm commitments on products and investment," said Resch, who also sits on the carmaker's supervisory board. Regular rounds of cost-cutting and unreliable commitments are eroding trust and the company "needs to take responsibility and say what future it plans for its German sites," she added.

With worker representatives holding half the seats on supervisory boards at large German automakers, labor holds significant sway over decisions including factory investments and restructuring. Powerful works councils and collective bargaining agreements add another layer of involvement in changes to jobs, working hours and plant operations.

That influence is being tested as Germany's auto industry confronts one of its most difficult periods in decades. Manufacturers are struggling with weak demand in Europe and China, intense competition from Chinese rivals and the costly transition to electric vehicles, while high labor and production costs have increased pressure on German factories.

These challenges have intensified a debate over who should shoulder the burden of restructuring. Automakers argue they can no longer afford long-standing benefits, while unions and works councils say employees are being asked to pay for strategic mistakes.

At both Mercedes and Volkswagen AG, management is seeking to extend the 35-hour workweek without extra pay and freeze wages for two years. IG Metall officials at VW have called the demands a "catalog of horrors," saying the company also wants to cut profit-sharing, scrap supplemental payments and eliminate a paid break for some shift workers.

The union's sharper rhetoric coincides with a wave of 24-hour stoppages it has organized Friday, part of a separate nationwide dispute with manufacturing companies over pay, benefits and working hours. The escalation is set to disrupt activity at companies already under pressure from weak demand, high costs and tougher global competition.

The union's rhetoric comes with a wave of 24-hour work stoppages that it organized on Friday as part of a nationwide dispute with companies over pay, benefits and working hours. It's something we actually told you about yesterday, and the escalation is expected to disrupt activity at companies that are already under pressure from weak demand, rising costs and strong global competition.

#5783. Restoring trust: Embattled CDC, HHS officials on their priorities for 2027

Restoring trust: Embattled CDC, HHS officials on their priorities for 2027" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Federal health officials are focused on rebuilding trust with the public and working across the aisle with the new Congress.

Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Director Erica Schwartz, M.D., and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., spoke at the Milken Institute’s Future of Health Summit last week in Washington, D.C. Over 1,200 attendees gathered at the event, the theme of which was “better health within reach.”

In a fireside chat, a chipper Schwartz tried to answer a tough line of questioning about Americans’ loss of trust in her agency, controversial vaccine changes, measles and other public health issues.

When asked about her potential disagreements with Kennedy, Schwartz said, “I disagree all the time. He’s a lawyer, I’m a lawyer. […] What I love about the secretary is that he listens to those disagreements. He's not someone who just says, ‘No, I don't have room for that.’ He really does value differing opinions.”

The U.S. has lost its measles elimination status, global health officials announced just this week. On that issue, Schwartz stressed the importance of supporting CDC’s state partners on awareness, prevention and surveillance efforts.

“MMR is the number one way to prevent measles,” Schwartz said. Today’s outbreaks “happen in communities that are very close-knit communities … that typically do not and have not vaccinated their children,” she said. Most cases are currently among kids over the age of five and adults, according to Schwartz.

Under Schwartz’s leadership, the CDC changed its method of reporting measles deaths from real-time reporting by state public health departments to death certificate data, which can face multi-month lags. Schwartz is being investigated by Energy & Commerce Committee Democrats who, during a briefing on CDC’s alleged suppression of the total number of national measles deaths on its dashboard, have called her unresponsive and misleading.

“As the crisis worsens, we are concerned that you continue to direct an effort at CDC to downplay the outbreak and artificially reduce the number of measles deaths that CDC reports to the public, concealing the fact that 10 people have died of measles-related deaths this year alone,” the Committee leaders wrote (PDF) in a letter on Tuesday. “We are expanding our investigation to examine the threat your actions pose to Americans’ health and whether changes to your statutory authority are required.”

During her fireside chat, Schwartz acknowledged that "we've lost trust not only externally with the American public, but also internally with the team that works at the CDC,” she said. To address this, Schwartz wants the public to understand that CDC follows the science, is being transparent and “leading with humility.” She pointed to COVID-era “arrogance” from institutions, directing at instead of conversing with the public.

“I want to be a CDC director that really has a conversation with the American public,” Schwartz said.

Internally, the first priority is to add stability to the body, including hiring leaders within the agency so they have a permanent leadership role. The CDC has also created a strategic hiring plan for 2027 with the input of staff and is looking to its “force extenders” like epidemic intelligence officers and its Public Health Associate Program.

On how she’s planning to work with the new majority-Democratic Congress, Schwartz noted she was encouraged to see more Congress members coming in with a healthcare background, “who understand how these policies will impact patients.” She said is eager to work with the Congressional Doctors Caucus and to work with both sides of the aisle.

“I know that we may not agree on every issue, but I do think there's a common ground where we can actually focus on really trying to make Americans healthy again,” she said.

One of her priorities for 2027 is having a “21st-century CDC” by bringing innovation into the public health sphere. She called out the Biothreat Radar, a proposed wastewater surveillance program about which she recently spoke with Sen. Andy Kim (D-New Jersey). The program’s proposed (PDF) budget is $52 million. The CDC has also tentatively put out a call for new Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) members, which will depend on a final ruling from the appellate court in the agency’s favor.

At the Summit, Schwartz’s comments did not necessarily satisfy some of the attendees. When asked by Fierce Healthcare for his impressions of the interview, a public health worker in the room who did not wish to be named called her a “traitor."

In his fireside chat closing out the Summit, Secretary Kennedy primarily spoke about food and obesity.

One of HHS' most consequential accomplishments during his tenure, Kennedy said, has been changing the dietary guidelines to be “science-based.” Earlier this year, the White House released new federal dietary guidelines, calling for prioritizing quality protein, healthy fats, fruits, vegetables and whole grains, while avoiding highly processed foods and refined carbs.

The agency is focused on transforming food across a number of sectors, including in Head Start programs—free federal early childhood programs—which have received about $151 million in supplemental HHS awards to strengthen nutrition services. HHS is also focused on rolling out healthy food options in the military, Kennedy said, and within SNAP by allowing states to request waivers to restrict what SNAP dollars are spent on. As of this summer, HHS has launched a Make Hospital Food Healthier Pledge, challenging hospitals to put nutrition at the center of patient care. HHS has also encouraged medical schools to increase their number of education hours on nutrition from an average of two to 40 hours, Kennedy said.

“Real” food sales in grocery stores, Kennedy claimed, went up 8% this year, while obesity rates have dropped by 7%. He acknowledged that the drop in obesity rates is more likely due to GLP-1 access rather than healthier eating. “If we can reduce obesity, we can reduce our healthcare costs,” he said, praising Trump’s Most Favored Nation negotiations for lowering the price of drugs like Ozempic.

“We reward people at every level—the hospitals, the providers, other providers, doctors, insurance companies, pharmaceutical companies—we reward them financially for keeping people sick. And as long as those financial incentives are in place, we are going to be operating a sick-care system rather than a healthcare system,” Kennedy said. HHS has started to change that by shifting more to value-based care, he added, so stakeholders get paid to keep patients healthy “rather than being paid to keep them sick.”

When asked what he wants his legacy as Health Secretary to be, Kennedy echoed Schwartz on the idea of following science. “What I want to do is to end corporate capture and the politicization of science … that Americans once again trust the regulatory agencies, they trust the science that’s coming from them,” he said.

He referred to newer guidelines meant to encourage extra transparency from researchers. In 2026, the HHS Scientific Integrity Policy was updated (PDF) to support publishing raw data and code in publicly accessible repositories, preregistering study protocols and transparently reporting all results.

He said he wants "to make sure that we’re not kowtowing to the food industry, the pharmaceutical industry, all these people who are at the trough taking on the $2.3 trillion that my agency gives out every year. And that instead, that Americans believe that this agency is devoted to their health, that they trust it, and that we are doing the science that we need to find out what is making them sick so that we can all eliminate it as a society.”

Kennedy's interview at the event did not touch on measles or vaccine policy, where the secretary's policies and communications have garnered broader criticism and controversy than his views on nutrition. Tuesday's announcement that the U.S. had lost its measles elimination status garnered a fresh call for Kennedy's resignation among his critics, including the Democratic Doctors Caucus.

Also coinciding with Milken's event was the announcement of the inaugural 2027 cohort of the Elevate Investment Initiative. The effort, part of the Milken Institute’s Women Health Network, aims to mobilize $1 billion in net-new capital for women’s health innovation. The 10 fund managers and companies include Borski Fund, Cross-Border Impact Ventures, Foreground Capital, Meridian Health Ventures, How Women Invest and more. [cut this or move?]

#5782. Is AI A Public Or A Private Asset?

Isabelle Ferreras is a professor and research director at the University of Louvain, an Accelerator fellow at the Institute for Ethics in AI at the University of Oxford, and a senior research associate at the Center for Labor and a Just Economy at Harvard University. It safe to say she knows a thing or two about computer technology and AI.

She told The Guardian this week that she has grave concerns about the way AI and the corporations promoting it are managing this brave new technology. Her concerns are spurred by the number of high profile computer engineers who have quit recently over fears that AI development is out of control.

Last month, a person responsible for overseeing safety reports at OpenAI left the company, claiming its culture was “broken.” He added that the entire AI industry was careless when it comes to developing AI technology. The month before that, a researcher at Anthropic — which went public yesterday at a valuation $1.8 trillion dollars — warned that AI “could kill us all by the end of the decade.”

“When the only way for a conscientious engineer to raise the alarm is to leave,” Ferreras said. “it is a clear sign that corporate governance in the industry is broken. Each departure takes with it the very knowledge needed to steer these systems safely. We cannot regulate AI safely from the outside if the companies building it remain autocracies on the inside.”

Ferreras warned that governments think of AI either as a “consumer product to be tested for defects or as a geopolitical race to be won by relaxing rules on business. Corporate lobbyists encourage this view as a trade-off between safety and innovation by arguing that legislation imposes too many burdens.

“This is a dangerous path. AI is not merely a software product. It is a technology of government. Yet inside frontier labs such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft, and Google, a handful of executives and capital investors decide which values are coded into models that shape millions of lives,” she said.

Interestingly, Michael Connolly, the award winning author of the Bosch and Lincoln Lawyer novels, published a book last year in which the family of a young woman, who was murdered by her boyfriend after he interacted with an AI agent, sues the company behind the AI agent. The essence of the lawsuit is that AI only does what it is programmed to do, and since the lead programmer of this particular AI agent was a misogynist in real life, it reflected his values when it interacted with humans. The book is called The Proving Ground and it is a fascinating read.

While Ferreras applauds those who warn of the malignancies built into AI, she pointed out that humans have short attention spans. “Time and again, a safety researcher or engineer walks out of the door with a public warning that commercial pressures are overriding safety guardrails. As a society, we applaud the courage of these individuals and debate their warnings for a news cycle — and then we move on. But we miss the deeper institutional failure those resignations reveal. As the great political scientist Albert Hirschman made clear, exit is not voice.”

In a democratic society, the exercise of governing power requires the consent of the governed, Ferreras told The Guardian. “Yet corporate law still treats firms as the property of shareholders, and the labor investors, who put their intellect, health and lives into the firm, as subordinates. To align AI with the public interest, we need a dual strategy: alongside solid public regulations on AI ‘from the outside,’ we need to enter the corporate black box and force corporate governance into alignment with democratic principles.”

An analogy can be made to the Federal Communications Commission, which licenses broadcasters and promotes the free flow of information to the public. The digital world thinks such controls are archaic, but the lack of them is a clear and present danger to a civil society.

Ferreras suggested that “governments must outlaw non-disclosure and non-disparagement clauses that silence staff on safety risks, and enact robust whistle blower protection. Tech workers also need a collective standing over corporate strategy, independent channels to report safety breaches, and formal representation inside frontier labs before models are deployed.”

In addition, she argued that “legislators must establish a binding right to co-decision over workplace AI. No algorithmic system that monitors, evaluates or disciplines workers should be deployed without prior negotiation. At national and EU level, we need to consider collective bargaining on AI deployment and veto rights for works councils or trade unions, backed by independent technical experts and a strict ban on automated firing.”

Lastly, she supported the democratization of boardrooms and rewarding firms that refuse to concentrate power at the top. “Legislators should mandate worker-elected directors on boards, moving towards dual-majority governance in which strategic decisions require the consent not only of capital but of labor.” Some, like Elon Musk and Mark Zuckerberg, would characterize her suggestions as liberal claptrap, and they would be correct. Ferreras would happily unravel the “tech bro” manosphere in order to promote a more open and just society.

She pointed to the research by Daron Acemoglu and Simon Johnson, the 2024 Nobel laureates in economics, which demonstrates that technological revolutions do not automatically produce shared prosperity. Instead, institutions decide who benefits and who pays.

“Extending democracy into the firm is not an old battle over power for its own sake, but a practical necessity for more ethical judgment. Aligning AI with the good of workers and society requires more wisdom than closed executive rooms can offer. It needs what the Yale political theorist Hélène Landemore calls ‘democratic reason’ — the collective intelligence of diverse, deliberating voices, brought to bear on corporate decision-making,” Ferreras wrote.

“Left to self-regulation and the occasional whistleblower, AI governance will entrench an unaccountable algorithmic oligarchy. Accountability and alignment begins with giving those who build these systems and those whose work they govern an enforceable voice, from the code floor to the boardroom.”

Ferreras’ point of view is decidedly liberal, and yet her arguments are clear and concise. How can we give so much power to digital agents and not take reasonable steps to ensure the needs of society as a whole are respected? The tech industry enjoys almost unfettered freedom of action today. It may be time to consider whether that is a good long term strategy.

The reproduction data plate reveals the GT500KR was indeed a Wimbledon White example from the factory, and the blue stripes were added later by a previous owner. The cabin is done in black knit-insert vinyl, covering both the front buckets and the Sport Deck rear seat. It also features the Interior Décor Group, which brings woodgrain accents to the dash, console, and doors, as well as the Visibility Group, which adds under-dash courtesy lamps along with lights for the glovebox, trunk, and engine bay.

A 2017 inspection report of the car by Kevin Marti highlights past rust repair and some Bondo. Notably, the battery-tray fender apron isn't original. According to the description, the car's engine and transmission were resealed in 2016, and in June of 2017, California emissions equipment was added. The seller mentions that the fuel cap, antenna, and fuel door were replaced recently, as were the starter and starter solenoid. #5780. Two Tuberculosis Regimens Containing Novel Agents Show Promise

— Phase II platform trial's design could speed development of new combinations for TB

Two four-drug regimens that combined new agents with commonly used drugs showed promise in tuberculosis (TB), and should be evaluated further, results from a phase II trial suggested.

The time to positivity slope -- the rate of change from baseline to week 12 in the time to Mycobacterium tuberculosis growth in a positive sputum culture, with a steeper time indicating faster TB clearance -- was 0.129 log10 (days) per week with investigational ganfeborole plus bedaquiline, pretomanid, and moxifloxacin (BPMG) and 0.142 log10 (days) per week with investigational BTZ-043 plus bedaquiline, delamanid, and moxifloxacin (BDMT), as compared with 0.118 log10 (days) per week with standard isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol (HRZE), for relative differences of 9.1% and 20.5%, respectively.

The posterior probability of superiority was 0.83 and 0.99 with the BPMG and BDMT regimens versus HRZE, reported Nicholas Paton, MD, of National University of Singapore, and colleagues in the New England Journal of Medicine.

At week 48, 80% of those in the BPMG group and 93% of those in the BDMT group had favorable-outcome status compared with 89% of the HRZE group.

"Our findings show the potential of large-scale, early-phase clinical trials for evaluating multiple regimens simultaneously with a design that permits the use of early data on treatment failure or relapse to inform selection of regimens for further evaluation," Paton and colleagues wrote.

The four-drug combinations will move on to testing in the phase II trial's second stage.

In an accompanying editorial, Eric Rubin, MD, PhD, of the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health in Boston, cautioned that the number of new TB agents in the development pipeline "creates a combinational nightmare."

This study outlines "a potentially very useful approach to prioritizing which regimens should be tested in very long and expensive phase III trials," Rubin noted. "The use of phase II trials with a design similar to that of the current trial might get some of these new agents into later-phase clinical trials more rapidly."

Despite the encouraging results, it's not clear whether they will lead to improved TB outcomes, he added. "Although almost all drug combinations can kill the bulk of bacteria, a small subpopulation seems to be responsible for the lengthy regimens that are necessary to cure all patients," Rubin wrote. The trial's time-to-positivity results "most likely tell us more about the bulk population than about the rarer bacteria that might survive for extended times."

While the current trial "provides useful guidelines for prioritizing late-phase trials," those later trials will still be critical, he pointed out. Referencing the movie "The Princess Bride," Rubin reminded investigators and clinicians alike that, "as Miracle Max says, 'You rush a miracle man, you get rotten miracles.'"

The PARADIGM-4TB adaptive platform trial assigned participants with rifampin-susceptible pulmonary TB to receive standard HRZE for 24 weeks; bedaquiline, delamanid, and moxifloxacin for 16 weeks; or one of 10 new four-drug combinations for 16 weeks. The new regimens contained ganfeborole, BTZ-043, or both, with combinations of bedaquiline, delamanid, moxifloxacin, pyrazinamide, pretomanid, and linezolid.

Ganfeborole blocks an enzyme essential to mycobacterial protein synthesis, while BTZ-043 inhibits an essential enzyme in cell-wall synthesis.

The study enrolled 401 adults at 14 clinical sites in South Africa, Tanzania, Uganda, Vietnam, and Moldova. Patients had TB symptoms or chest radiography evidence, as well as a medium or high semiquantitative result on the Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra assay. Patients with HIV were excluded. Median patient age was 30 years, 84% were male, 68% had a high bacterial load, and 77% had cavitation on a chest radiograph.

Severe adverse events occurred in 38% of the BPMG group, 28% of the BDMT group, and 24% of the HRZE group. Among the trial's 118 patients who had a serious adverse event, 45% had a decrease from baseline in creatinine clearance, "which contributed to excess severe adverse events in some new-regimen groups," Paton and team noted. Most of those patients had creatinine clearance fall by more than 30%.

Study limitations included the open-label design and the small sizes of each treatment group. Time to positivity is a surrogate endpoint that hasn't always predicted clinical endpoints, the authors cautioned. While the study population included only those with rifampin-susceptible TB, any treatments' target clinical population would include patients with rifampin-resistant TB.

HLTH 2026: American Hospital Association, West Health Institute announce new collaboration with BD" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The American Hospital Association (AHA) and West Health Institute announced Tuesday a new collaboration with medtech company Becton, Dickinson and Company (BD) aimed at accelerating the adoption of technologies shown to improve patient care.

The collaboration builds on the West Health Accelerator at AHA’s Health Research & Educational Trust (HRET), a three-year initiative to aid healthcare organizations in scaling technology-enabled solutions.

“No single organization can close the gap between innovation and everyday care on its own,” said Zia Agha, M.D., West Health Institute chief medical officer, in a statement. “This collaboration brings hospital reach, clinical technology expertise and performance intelligence together from the start. The new collaboration will begin with an initial cohort of 10 hospitals and health systems. It will incorporate advanced physiologic monitoring with clinical protocols in practice, specifically targeting issues associated with postoperative complications and longer hospital stays. Additionally, Vizient will provide performance benchmarking and analytic capabilities, the organizations said.

Takeaways from the early cohort will help to identify adoption barriers, refine implementation approaches and outline necessary support to expand the model to a broader group.

BD Advanced Patient Monitoring Worldwide President Tim Patz said in a statement that the company believes innovation “has the greatest impact when it translates into meaningful improvements in patient care.”

“Our experience working with healthcare systems has shown us the value of bringing together advanced hemodynamic monitoring, data and the expertise of hospital care teams to support better-informed patient care,” Patz said. “This collaboration gives us an opportunity to build on that experience, further integrate proven solutions into clinical practice and help more patients benefit from them.”

#5778. Stellantis Is Pulling Out Of Every Racing Series It Competes In Except NASCAR

Stellantis is about to throw in the towel on just about every single one of its motorsports endeavors other than NASCAR... which it just re-entered after a 14-year hiatus. On November 23, it's expected that the automaker will convene two extraordinary works council meetings with the ultimate outcome being a withdrawal. That means Peugeot would leave endurance racing (which admittedly hasn't been going too well), Citroën and Opel would drop out of Formula E, and Lancia's reborn rally team would bite the dust.

The moves come as the automaker cuts costs across the board at the behest of CEO Antonio Filosa, according to Reuters. He's doing what he can to turn the company around after years of falling sales and weakening profitability. Earlier this year, Filosa launched a broad efficiency drive, known as the "Value Creation Program," and it targets about $6.6 billion in cost savings by 2028. Autocar reports that Stellantis Motorsport costs about $330 million a year to run, and cutting it could help with Stellantis' finances in Europe, where it just lost $341 million in the third quarter alone.

This isn't the first time something like this has happened for Peugeot. Its former owners, PSA, quit the 24 Hours of Le Mans back in 2012 in an effort to save cash, and it didn't rejoin until 2022.

It is, nevertheless, still strange timing. As I mentioned, Dodge just re-entered NASCAR. On top of that, French outlet L'Automobile reports that Peugeot has a redesigned 9x8 for its 2027 WEC endurance program and Citroën and Opel have been working on their new Gen4 car for Formula E with new technical partners. It's likely that the team that runs Citroën, MSG Racing, will continue with a new sponsor.

Hell, Open is technically making its debut in FE this upcoming season. It was just announced in March of this year when the brand signed a four-year contract to compete with the new Gen4 cars.

Lancia's WRC re-entry is another sacrificial lamb at the altar of financial prudence. The Lancia Corse HF team started in the WRC2 category this year, Autocar reports. It entered its gas-powered Ypsilon Rally2 HF Integrale, and it has even racked up a few wins. More likely than not, customer teams will continue to be supported, though.

Motorsports are usually what's first to get cut when an automaker is struggling. Earlier this year, Alpine dropped out of WEC, citing a tough market, and Porsche did the same thing back in 2025.

#5777. The Metals Company Has a Seabed Mining Production Gap That Its Pilot Has Not Closed

In 2022, The Metals Company (TMC) and offshore contractor Allseas recovered 3,021 wet tons of nodules from the Pacific seabed. Their integrated test system moved material up a riser stretching more than four kilometres from the ocean floor to the Hidden Gem. During production runs, the collector achieved 86.4 wet tons per hour. Four years later, TMC is discussing a million tons a year from an upgraded system and eventually 12 million tons annually across four vessels.

What matters between those endpoints is the operating record: sustained collection rates, marine maintenance, vessel availability and delivered tons sufficient to carry fixed costs. TMC has yet to demonstrate those economics.

The November 12, 2026 corporate update describes a phased approach: begin with an upgraded pilot collector and limited modifications to Hidden Gem, then invest in larger systems as operations develop. Phasing reduces the initial capital commitment. It also pushes the demonstration of the projected commercial production rates into the future.

The annual arithmetic is straightforward. At 5,000 productive hours, about 57% of a calendar year, a system collecting 200 wet tons per hour delivers one million tons. The second-year target of 1.5 million tons requires 300 tons per hour. Three million tons from one production system requires 600 tons per hour. TMC’s 2022 production-run rate of 86.4 tons per hour would deliver 432,000 tons at that utilization.

The upgraded machines are expected to be different from the 2022 test collector. Their performance must be demonstrated, not assumed from the pilot. The operating gap is central to the project economics, and it grows with production ambitions.

The full TFIE Strategy Briefing examines TMC’s production gap alongside Impossible Metals’ autonomous collection model and the investment consequences of underperforming equipment. The source assessment and fleet sensitivities are linked there.

A collector, a multi-kilometre hydraulic riser and a production vessel have to work together. The crawler encounters uneven ground and varying nodule coverage. The riser and pumps handle abrasive slurry. The vessel must remain on station while crews inspect, maintain and repair equipment. Offshore access and weather affect when those activities can occur.

A system can produce at its test rate and still lose the year on maintenance and interruptions. Fewer productive hours push the required hourly rate higher. Repeating a successful short production run does not establish a year’s availability, let alone multiple years of fleet productivity.

The difference matters because capital and offshore operating costs continue while production is interrupted. Ships, crews, marine maintenance equipment and financing cost money whether or not nodules are arriving on deck. Smaller annual production spreads fixed expenses over fewer tons and raises the cost of every ton recovered.

TMC’s August 2025 prefeasibility presentation estimated offshore collection and transport at $179 per dry ton, or about $129 per wet ton under its 28% moisture assumption. Those are projections for a future system. They are not an audited cost record from continuous industrial mining. The revised first-production configuration needs its own cost data.

The missing commercial evidence is a long enough operating record to estimate productive hours, rate degradation, planned and unplanned maintenance, retrieval time, replacement costs and the delivered cost per ton. Until then, moving from a pilot to a production forecast remains a major assumption.

Impossible Metals proposes to collect individual nodules with autonomous underwater vehicles rather than a tracked crawler and riser. A vehicle would descend, select nodules, fill its cargo compartment, return, undergo surface recovery, unload and prepare for another mission. Every trip must be repeated across an entire fleet.

Its September 2026 scientific trial, reported by Reuters, recovered approximately 450 grams of nodules from more than 4,000 metres depth. It demonstrated selective scientific collection. A commercial robot would have to carry vastly more material and sustain cycle times and availability that the experiment did not measure.

In the 2025 commercial concept examined by metallurgical specialist Lyle Trytten and me, each proposed vehicle carried 12 tons of nodules and had 18 collection arms. At one nodule every 1.5 seconds per arm and an average nodule mass of 100 grams, filling the cargo requires roughly 120,000 successful picks. With all arms continuously working, collection alone occupies approximately 2.8 hours.

The proposed complete mission cycle was four hours. Descent, ascent, searching, repositioning, failed picks, recovery, unloading, inspection and relaunch also consume time. The architecture has too many interdependent activities to fit those requirements into that cycle at the assumed performance.

Autonomous navigation and manipulator tests cannot substitute for evidence of an entire fleet repeatedly executing commercial missions. Increasing payload changes vehicle weight, buoyancy, energy use and recovery equipment. Faster picking leaves the surface operation and deepwater transit to be solved.

Our 2025 independent techno-economic assessment tested the financial effects of weaker-than-assumed robot productivity. At the illustrative $180 per dry ton nodule sales value, the model required approximately $2.52 billion in capital with the originally assumed robot throughput. Halving throughput while maintaining output increased required capital to approximately $4.51 billion.

At a 10% discount rate, the modeled net present value moved from positive $863 million to negative $769 million. Even at two-thirds of original productivity, NPV fell to about $15 million, a negligible margin for a multibillion-dollar first-of-a-kind industrial fleet.

These are scenario calculations, not actual bills or calibrated probabilities. They identify the key failure mode: more robots, recovery capacity, batteries, vessels and maintenance are needed to compensate for each production shortfall. A financial model based on high productivity can look attractive until realistic availability and turnaround times are included.

TMC is further along technologically than Impossible Metals, but its future-scale production economics are also unsupported by a sustained operating record. Neither company has demonstrated the productive hours, throughput and maintenance costs needed to support its advertised commercial proposition.

Policymakers and investors should ask for extended end-to-end offshore operating records and audited unit economics before treating future production targets as investable output. The technology risk exists before accounting for nodule processing, metals markets, permitting or environmental liabilities.

The complete TFIE Briefing and linked assessment show the fleet calculations, technical assumptions and capital sensitivities. The remaining articles in the five-part series address processing, metals markets and American Samoa’s exposure.

#5776. F1 Finally Hiring Permanent Race Stewards, Replacing Volunteer Officials

Unlike the typical ball sports, a significant number of on-track rule infractions are strictly tied to a specific penalty. The punishment is selected from a set range by part-time volunteers who are often criticized by drivers, teams and fans for their inconsistency. The Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile announced on Thursday that it will be introducing full-time stewards to officiate Formula 1 next season. The sport's global governing body is finally shedding one of the last vestiges of its aristocratic past, aiming to provide more consistent rule calls. Welcome to 21st century, F1.

The transition to full-time professional officials likely won't be completed by the start of the 2027 season. The FIA stated it's establishing a department of 12 to 15 full-time stewards recruited from its existing pool of international stewards. While they will initially complement the current part-timers, the role of the permanent stewards will expand as their roster grows. Beyond officiating F1 race weekends, the full-timers will form a constant rule-decision base and train their eventual successors with those precedents. FIA President Mohammed Ben Sulayem said:

"This latest major investment in FIA officiating reflects our dedication to delivering the highest standards of decision-making, fairness and integrity in motorsport. The recruitment of full-time stewards is a significant step in our longstanding mission of building a dedicated officiating ecosystem in the FIA Formula One World Championship, it is also an investment in the future of our sport."

Formula 1 was formed in the same aristocratic primordial pool of international sports that encouraged the International Olympic Committee to ban professional athletes until 1986. European aristocrats held the reins of international motorsport until that same period. Prince Paul Alfons von Metternich-Winneburg finished a decade as FIA President in 1985. If the Metternich name sounds familiar, he was a great-grandson of Prince Klemens von Metternich, the influential 19th-century Austrian statesman.

While F1 has become a multi-billion-dollar enterprise, the championship's officiating has long remained locked in an era when amateurism was a virtue. As a result, the F1 stewards' office is filled with people who can afford to spend significant time and money earning the prerequisite credentials and gaining the necessary experience officiating smaller events. The unpaid volunteers are often successful lawyers and automotive executives, sometimes employed by companies directly involved in F1. Thankfully, those days are finally coming to an end.

#5775. Payer mix, non-labor expenses dragged hospital margins in September

Payer mix, non-labor expenses dragged hospital margins in September" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Hospitals’ operations took another dip in September amid a slew of ongoing headwinds including weakened payer mix and rising costs, healthcare advisory firm Kaufman Hall reported alongside warnings of a “historically large portion” of the nation’s hospitals running on negative or near-zero operating margins.

The firm’s latest monthly benchmark report, released Tuesday, showed a calendar year-to-date operating margin index of 1.4% and a single-month operating margin index of 2.4% in September, the latter of which was a decline from August’s 3.0% operating margin (all including health system allocations for shared services costs).

The performance decline wasn’t for want of patients. Daily discharges and adjusted discharges both rose 3% from August to September, and are generally above the numbers from last year. Operating room minutes per calendar day also rose 6% from August—an encouraging sign for hospitals whose surgical slowdowns had hamstrung acuity—but remain 1% below September of last year.

The increased foot traffic also grew revenues, with daily net operating revenue rising 4% from August and 6% year over year while gross operating revenue rose 4% month to month and 8% year over year. Much of the increase came on the outpatient side, where daily revenue increased 5% from August and 10% compared to September 2025. Net patient service revenue per adjusted discharge was more mixed, rising 2% from August but remaining 1% below September 2025.

However, hospitals’ margins are being challenged by persistent bad debt and charity care burdens, Kaufman Hall’s data show. Daily bad debt and charity care may have remained flat from August, but is 17% higher than September 2025 and 16% higher when comparing both years’ first nine months. As a percentage of gross operating revenue, they’re 6% higher than Sept. 2025 and 8% higher year to date.

On the spending side, daily total expense rose 3% from August and is 5% higher than September 2025, primarily reflecting the heightened volumes even as hospitals held their average length of stay flat month over month or 1% shorter year over year. The expenses were more pronounced on the non-labor side, where increases on a per adjusted discharge basis were higher than labor’s per adjusted discharge decline.

"Hospitals continue to operate in an environment marked by significant financial variability," Erik Swanson, managing director and Data and Analytics group leader at Kaufman Hall, said in a release. “Many organizations continue to face mounting pressure from uncompensated care and rising expenses, underscoring the importance of proactive operational and financial strategies that build long-term resilience."

Another amplifying market trend is the “bifurcation of hospital performance” often highlighted by the firm and others that monitor multi-organization financial trends, such as credit rating agencies.

"The margin gap between higher and lower-performing hospitals has widened to 19 percentage points, with a historically large portion of hospitals operating at negative or very thin margins,” the report reads. “Even slight revenue reductions threaten organizations, which face increasingly difficult decisions on future operations, care delivery, and expense control.”

The firm encouraged hospitals to take “deliberate, proactive steps” to strengthen their financial situations, particularly as macro reimbursement trends stiffen and the site of care delivery shifts from the hospital to outpatient settings.

Kaufman Hall’s hospital reports pull data from more than 1,300 nationwide hospitals as collected by parent company Strata Decision Technology.

Accompanying the monthly hospital benchmark was also Kaufman Hall’s quarterly numbers on more than 200,000 employed physicians and advanced practice providers, which painted a much rosier picture for health system and hospital employers.

It showed, for the first time in five years of data collection, that healthcare employers’ investment/subsidy per provider and per physician has declined year over year (by 1%), and “across every cohort, including primary care, medical specialty, surgical specialty and hospital-based specialty.”

Kaufman Hall attributed the rare turnaround to revenue growth and sustained productivity increases that together outpaced expenses.

"Medical groups made meaningful performance improvements this quarter, achieving gains in revenue, productivity and thoughtful workforce management," Matthew Bates, managing director and Physician Enterprise Service Line leader at Kaufman Hall, said in a release. "The growing utilization of [advanced practice providers] and ongoing focus on operational and team effectiveness are helping organizations manage financial pressures while increasing access to care.”

#5774. Electric Vans — Are They The Final EV Frontier? Kia PV5.

We took a trip to see the Kia PV5 electric van. Our brief takeaway: “Kool like a Kia.” Should keep the bean counters happy.

Inspired by a comment in the Electric Vehicle Council report about electric vans, Majella and I decided to have a short visit to a group of dealerships under the Norris Motors banner. We hoped to check out the LDV eDeliver 5 van, touted as selling for under AU$50,000. However, there was no stock to view and we ended up chatting to the dealer and then moving on to the MG U9 BEV ute. You can read about it here. And then we found the Kia PV5 delivery van.

Julie Delvecchio, the CEO of EVC, calls the lack of affordable electric vans in Australia “the single biggest unclaimed opportunity left.” We think that is about to change. Since its launch in May, 496 PV5 have sold in Australia.

The Kia PV5 reminded me a lot of the Renault Kangoo in both size and shape, and it is able to carry about the same payload. And the front looked like the BMW i3. The one we looked at had been sold and was awaiting a fitout as a camper van. The Norris Group Kia specialist was generous with his time and the information he shared. He has been selling the Kia EV5 for the past 5 months and delivered 5 of the vans. He sold his first one within a week of its arrival on the lot — to Ray, a driver working for Amazon.

Ray appreciated the 390 km range. My friendly sales rep tells me that this will be increased in 2027 models to 420 km. Ray was getting out of diesel and most of his questions were around charging and regen braking. Most of his trips were around the burbs and he was not intending to take the van on the highway. The Kia PV5 is a workhorse, with a passenger car feel and level of comfort. It even has electric lumbar support for the driver — great when you are spending so much time in the van delivering parcels in the lead-up to Christmas. It certainly has a lot more tech than the diesel he was trading in.

In fact, he was “blown away” by the standard features — the 360-degree camera, for example. “Vans are not known for their visibility.” On his return to the dealership for his first service, he commented on the smoothness of the torque: “It has no issues going uphill.” He reported that the van felt “well planted on the road.” Ray has gotten used to trickle charging at home and has lost his range anxiety. Like most new EV drivers, once he started living and working with the vehicle, his fears vanished. The PV5 supports fast charging also for when Ray needs a boost on the road.

But what about that all-important question of cost? Can we make the bean counters happy? The Kia PV5 retails for AU$56,000 (before on-road costs), which is about the same price as comparable diesel vans like the Ford Transit and the Toyota HiAce. Add to that the savings on fuel, the peace of mind from fuel security, and the reduced servicing and it is easy to build a business case for the Kia PV5 — cost per parcel delivery. The PV5 even comes with vehicle to load.

And it isn’t made in China! Can the PV5 replace Toyota’s HiAce? Find the answer in this video. The reviewer points out many features that make the PV5 an attractive option: the charge port is on the front. The van has lots of nooks and crannies for storage. She measures storage by capacity to fit in bottles of wine — for example, two in the glove box. There is a step provided to alight the van, aided by grab handles. More storage space is provided above the steering wheel, including a nifty phone slot. There are customizable buttons on the steering wheel to create shortcuts; for example, to the air conditioning settings. A wireless phone charger is nestled near the dash. The glovebox contains the V2L adaptor supplied with the van.

The fact that the van reverts to the lowest regen setting every time you restart the car is a little niggle. That, and there is no frunk — reducing the reviewer’s all-important need for wine storage. Full specs can be found here. Kia even gives you helpful advice on how to apply for electric vehicle subsidies (last page, bottom right). One of the pictures that caught my eye shows the PV5 as a flatbed truck.

The PV5 was recently named 2026 International Van of the Year. It measures 4695mm long, 2255mm wide, and 1899mm tall on a 2995mm wheelbase. Range is stated as 416 km, but will of course vary with driving style and load. The battery is a 71.2kWh nickel cobalt manganese (NCM) lithium-ion battery. Kia offers a 165,000 km warranty on the battery. The van is front-wheel drive.

The PV5 has over 4 cubic metres of cargo capacity, double both that of the ID Buzz and the Tesla Model Y. Space enough for two euro pallets. There are multiple access points, with sliding doors on both sides and barn doors in the rear. The rear barn doors open to 180 degrees, and a low 419mm load height improves accessibility.

Goods being shipped are protected by padding on the rear doors and insides of the back. The PV5 can carry up to 740 kg. Tiedowns on the floor of the rear of the van help to secure cargo. There is also a power point in the back of the van. Perhaps a tradie can recharge their tools on site. No frunk for wine.

From the spec sheet: “Standard driver assist features include blind-spot collision avoidance, navigation-based adaptive cruise control, lane-keep assist, lane centring with hands-on detection, and parking collision avoidance assist.”

A launch in the USA is financially difficult because of the 25% “chicken tax.” Kia builds the PV5 in South Korea and classifies it as a commercial vehicle, and it faces a 25% US import tariff on light trucks and commercial vans.

Sadly, the Kia PV5 doesn’t come in red, but only in white, grey and black. Most companies may take up the option of wrapping the van in their own livery. Overall, we were impressed with Kia PV5 and look forward to seeing more of them on the road throughout the suburbs as Australian delivery drivers move towards a bright electric future.
