#5773. Simple Lab Test May Predict Recurrence Risk in Most Common Type of Breast Cancer

— Higher eosinophil levels predicted better outcomes, better response to CDK4/6 inhibitors

Higher levels of circulating eosinophils had a significant association with improved recurrence-free survival (RFS) and distant metastasis-free survival (DMFS) in hormone receptor (HR)-positive breast cancer, a large retrospective analysis showed.

With an eosinophil cutoff of 0.08 × 109/L, patients with eosinophil counts above the cutoff had significantly better RFS (P=0.001) and DMFS (P=0.002). Higher levels of circulating eosinophils remained an independent predictor of improved outcomes in multivariable-adjusted statistical models. Reductions in the RFS and DMFS hazard ratios ranged between 50% and 60% before and after adjustment. The results were replicated in a large validation cohort of patients with HR-positive/HER2-negative breast cancer, albeit with smaller reductions in the hazard ratios.

Additionally, higher eosinophil counts predicted benefit from treatment with a CDK4/6 inhibitor, reported Zhi-Ming Shao, MD, PhD, of Fudan University Shanghai Cancer Center in China, and colleagues in the Journal of Clinical Oncology.

"Circulating eosinophil count is a robust prognostic biomarker, including during endocrine therapy," the authors stated. "Although the prognostic [hazard ratio] for eosinophil count differed between the discovery and expanded cohorts, this reflects differences in cohort design, case mix, and sample size; importantly, both estimates were directionally consistent, showing a protective effect."

"Second, [eosinophil count] provides significant additive prognostic value beyond the 21-gene risk score, suggesting that eosinophil levels in peripheral blood capture an immune dimension distinct from tumor genomics," they continued. "Third, eosinophils predict adjuvant CDK4/6 inhibitor efficacy, optimizing patient selection... . Importantly, the treatment-by-eosinophil interaction remained robust and the direction of effect was consistently protective across all analyses, supporting eosinophil count as a predictive biomarker regardless of absolute [hazard ratio] magnitude."

The findings add to previous studies showing that higher peripheral lymphocyte count and lower neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio are associated with better outcomes in early-stage breast cancer, primarily HR-negative subtypes, noted the authors of an accompanying editorial. Collectively, they highlight the biomarker potential of readily available laboratory parameters.

"None of these prognostic factors is in routine use, however, despite being readily available from a complete blood count for virtually every patient with breast cancer globally," wrote Peter Savas, MBBS, PhD, of Peter MacCallum Cancer Center in Melbourne, Australia, and Roberto Salgado, MD, PhD, of ZAS Hospitals in Antwerp, Belgium. "To achieve greater clinical relevance for circulating biomarkers, we can seek guidance from the success of risk-of-recurrence assays and the popularity of prognostic calculators such as PREDICT breast. These tools take a carefully considered approach to implementation, integrating standard clinicopathologic variables in a form that supports shared decision making and communication with patients."

"This should be the aim for any proposed biomarker that hopes to see widespread uptake, in addition to robust analytical and clinical validation."

HR-positive/HER2-negative breast cancer accounts for about two-thirds of all new cases of breast cancer, and despite treatment advances, late recurrence and distant relapse have persisted, the authors noted in their introduction. The absence of simple, noninvasive, blood-based biomarkers to monitor dynamic systemic immune status remains an unmet need. In particular, robust biomarkers to predict therapeutic benefit from CDK4/6 inhibitors have remained elusive, despite the drugs' established role in treating patients with HR-positive/HER2-negative breast cancer.

To date research into immune prognostic markers has focused primarily on tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes, ignoring the "prognostically relevant" myeloid compartment, the authors continued. To address the information void, investigators evaluated the prognostic potential of eosinophils, which previous studies have shown can prime antitumor T-cell responses. Investigators hypothesized that circulating eosinophil count could serve as a dynamic systemic marker of immune competence, distinct from tumor lymphoid infiltration.

Shao and colleagues retrospectively analyzed eosinophil counts in 472 patients with HR-positive/HER2-negative breast cancer treated with surgery and followed for a median of 83.1 months. The cohort had a median eosinophil count of 0.08 × 109/L. The cohort comprised 259 patients with eosinophil counts higher than the median and 213 with counts at the median or lower.

The data showed that patients with eosinophil counts exceeding the median had a 54% lower hazard for RFS (95% CI 0.28-0.77) and a 56% lower hazard for DMFS (95% CI 0.25-0.78). Multiple variable analyses produced hazard ratios of 0.49 (P=0.007) and 0.50 (P=0.017) for RFS and DMFS, respectively. Among 406 patients treated with endocrine therapy, higher eosinophil counts predicted better RFS (HR 0.41, 95% CI 0.24-0.70, P=0.001) and DMFS (HR 0.39, 95% CI 0.21-0.72, P=0.002).

To evaluate the functional impact of circulating eosinophil infiltration, the investigators implanted eosinophils into the mammary fat pads of mouse models of HR-positive/HER2-negative breast cancer. The results showed significantly reduced tumor growth in animals that received eosinophils versus those that did not.

Finally, Shao and colleagues investigated circulating eosinophils' association with RFS and DMFS in a validation cohort of 23,177 patients, 10,488 with eosinophil counts exceeding the median and 10,689 with values at or below the median. They had a median follow-up of 32.6 months. The high-eosinophil group had a statistically significant 17% lower risk of distant metastasis (95% CI 0.70-0.99, P=0.034). The association remained significant in a multivariable analysis that included age, nodal status, tumor size, and Ki67 value.

A separate analysis of 3,471 high-risk patients treated with adjuvant CDK4/6 inhibitors showed that the therapy improved DMFS overall, but patients with higher eosinophil counts derived greater benefit (HR 0.25, 95% CI 0.12-0.48, P<0.0001) than those with lower counts (HR 0.59, 95% CI 0.38-0.93, P=0.022).

#5772. The Benz-Branded Mercedes SL Is Coming Back

When Mercedes introduced the seventh-generation R232 SL roadster, it was only offered in performance-oriented AMG trims, with an ultra-luxury Maybach variant coming a few years later. For the first time in the model's history, a Benz-branded SL was missing from the lineup, but that's about to change because of buyer feedback. Some folks apparently miss the subdued, grand touring nature that SLs of old provided, and they don't all have the $230,000 it takes to enter Maybach land, so a Mercedes-Benz SL is coming back.

With this current generation, Mercedes wanted to bring the SL and AMG GT Coupe closer together, and it seems that may have been a slight miscalculation on the German automaker's part. While big power and big prices are all well and good, it's not exactly what the average SL owner is looking for — especially when the Mercedes-AMG GT Coupe exists, according to Autocar. They missed some of the refinement and long-distance cruising ability of the old cars. Basically, the new one was hurting their agining backs.

Now that its mid-cycle refresh time, the GT will remain the performance-oriented vehicle, and the SL will take on a more relaxed demeaner, CEO Ola Källenius told Autocar. It'll trade in rock hard suspension and track times for comfort and ride quality. The two vehicles will also get revised engines to meet new emissions standards in Communist Europe.

Mercedes will discontinue the entry-level SL43 and GT43 that use a turbocharged 2.0-liter inline-4, and the same fate will befall the SL63 S E Performance and its 805-horsepower plug-in-hybrid V8 powertrain. Instead, the updated SLs will all get 48-volt mild-hybrid systems, and the new entry-level engine is expected to be a 443-hp turbocharged 3.0-liter inline-6, which is far more befitting of a grand tourer anyway. That model will probably be called SL500, while an SL580 will have the new M177 Evo flat-plane crank V8 we first saw in the refreshed S-Class.

Don't worry, drop-top AMG fans. The AMG SL isn't going anywhere, even if the E Performance is. Autocar speculates that the M177 will be also used in an SL63 that'll put out a notch over 600 horsepower, which should be more than enough for the folks who are into things of that nature. (The AMG SL55 will effectively be replaced by the V8 Benz SL580.)

It's not just an ethos change, either. Mercedes says the Benz SL will have front-end styling that alighes closer with the standard Mercedes look, with a simpler grille that has one horizontal bar across it rather than the more aggressive AMG grille with all its vertical canes. It'll also make use of the latest Digital Light headlight system from the company, which, of course, features three-pointed-star daytime running lights. Inside, the car will get an upgraded MB.OS platform to run the infotainment and the rest of the car's brain as well as some new physical control.

If this all sounds exciting to you in a way that the AMG SL didn't, well, you've got to hold on just a little bit longer. Källenius says the refreshed SL, which is going to be "more of a Mercedes-Benz," is expected to lauch in 2027.

#5771. HLTH 2026 Daily Tracker: F1 mania takes over HLTH; Why DJ Steve Aoki is investing in innovative science

HLTH 2026 Daily Tracker: F1 mania takes over HLTH; Why DJ Steve Aoki is investing in innovative science" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The Fierce Healthcare team is on the ground at HLTH 2026. Stick with this news tracker to catch all the highlights from the show floor, and click here for additional coverage from the conference.

DJ and music producer Steve Aoki told the HLTH audience that his father's passing was the catalyst for his interest in healthcare.

Learning more about what caused his death, and if it could have been prevented, drew him to the impacts of dementia and cancer. And in exploring that, he said he decided he wanted to invest in the people who are pursuing the "science fiction concepts" in healthcare, and support cutting edge innovation.

Aoki said that his celebrity status made it easier to get into a room with people leading the charge on innovation, and learn as much as he could.

"I was just as intrigued as working with a big artist in the studio or playing a big show," he said.

It was with that learning that he established Aoki Foundation, an organization he said is dedicated to bringing back the science and investing in what's next.

"People are excited about science fiction, about the possibility of doing things that are impossible," Aoki said. "And I feel like the superheroes of our time are like right right in our midst, and it's about it's about highlighting their journey and giving them a spotlight."

It’s been several weeks since Doximity integrated Wolters Kluwer Health’s UpToDate into its AI clinical decision support tool.

Doximity VP of Clinical AI Partnerships Kamal Menghrajani, M.D., told Fierce Healthcare at HLTH said the integration gives her “a little bit more confidence” in her own practice.

“Now I can use UpToDate to supplement and feel like what I'm doing at the point of care really is the best thing for the patient,” she said.

Menghrajani, who previously served as assistant director for cancer innovation and public health at the White House, took on the role with Doximity approximately four months ago.

“[I get to] be the physician voice and represent the interests of doctors within the company,” she said. “And think about what it looks like to actually take the tools we're building and serve doctors better.”

Menghrajani said the rapid expansion of the company’s AI suite has been a key takeaway, adding that a focus for the company is what physicians want out of AI. “I've seen Doximity evolve to meet all of those needs,” Menghrajani said.

As a range of AI tools saturate the industry, Menghrajani said the biggest use she has seen amongst clinicians is ambient scribes. “I think that has been a real game changer in terms of actual practice,” she said.

On the HLTH show floor, you may have noticed a theme.

Las Vegas is abuzz with the upcoming Formula 1 race, which is taking place on Saturday, Nov. 21. The city has been preparing for the Las Vegas Grand Prix, which is on the Strip, for weeks, and HLTH is taking place at one of the hubs for F1 excitement, The Venetian.

So at this year's conference, each of the stages is themed around racing: the Velocity Stage, the Ferrari Stage, the Monacco Stage. And each breakout track is referred to as a "circuit." In the conference livery, HLTH mascot Petunia is show driving a race car.

Activations on the show floor also play into the F1 theme. A racing simulation game is set up for attendees near the Pharma Force stage, and swag giveaways allude to the race.

Panelists at a HLTH session discussing the uptake of ICHRA — scratch that, CHOICE — faced a challenge around the nomenclature.

Individual coverage health reimbursement arrangements, or ICHRAs, represent a growing area of interest for employers and insurers participating in the individual market. But on Sept. 3, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services announced that it would instead refer to these models as CHOICE, which stands for Custom Health Option and Individual Care Expense.

In these models, an employer offers enrollees a stipend to purchase coverage on the individual market rather than securing a traditional employer-sponsored plan. ICHRA (or CHOICE) has gained traction with employers that may otherwise struggle to offer health coverage.

Moderator Joseph Mercer, senior managing director at Marwood Group, joked that the panelists had all agreed to call these plans CHOICE rather than ICHRA. But throughout the session, slip-ups drew a chuckle.

Even the panel's title made reference to the evolution of the name: "The ICHRA (CHOICE) Debate."

Healthcare platform Simple HealthKit announced Tuesday a partnership with Waters Corporation to expand access to at-home cervical cancer screening.

The collaboration aims to expand access to BD’s Onclarity HPV Self-Collection Kit, which is tested with the BD Onclarity HPV Assay  and Simple HealthKit's artificial intelligence-powered direct-to-patient-provider platform.

"We envision a future where personalized, world-class healthcare is accessible to everyone, regardless of where they live,” said Sheena Menezes, Ph.D, Simple HealthKit CEO and co-founder, in a statement. “Our AI-powered direct-to-patient and provider platform brings that vision to life by connecting people with the right education, intelligent personalized engagement, and clinical care at every step.”

Menezes continued, “Through partnerships with innovators like Waters Corporation, we are empowering individuals to take charge of their health while making seamless, personalized care accessible at scale.”

Oura CEO joined Counsel Health CEO and founder Muthu Alagappan Tuesday morning to discuss the wearable company’s recently announced $625 million acquisition of the virtual primary care company.

Hale said Oura selected Counsel as a partner after reviewing the landscape, and “uptake” from customers was “very positive.”

“We started talking seriously about taking that partnership,” Hale said. “And while we had been dating for a while, we thought maybe it was time to get married.”

Hale said the agreement was “really driven” by Oura customers using Counsel in “really novel and interesting ways.”

Alagappan said one of the most exciting aspects of the partnership is the potential impact of AI-fueled access to physicians on preventive care, adding the daily engagement of wearing Oura rings struck him.

“The buy-in from almost all users is tremendous, and so you enable primary care with the thing that has always been missing, which is engagement,” he said. “And now we have a way to incentivize, motivate patients to make the changes that actually prevent disease, alongside the screenings and lab tests that are also very important.”

During a Monday fireside chat, CMS Deputy Administrator and Chief Product Officer Amy Gleason said HHS and OCR colleagues “have done an amazing job” at looking at the issue to “remove friction from the patient experience.”

Gleason said there are three main components of the rule: the designation of a “personal health app,” identity verification and speed. “It should be almost instantaneous with electronic data, and it also says that this information is free to the patient,” she said.

Throughout the session with Zus Health CEO and co-founder Jonathan Bush, Gleason also touted the agency’s voluntary CMS Health Tech Ecosystem initiative.

“The idea of this was to stop waiting on regulation, like healthcare does for some reason, and to just charge forward and get the technology and people that are willing to go faster to work on it,” Gleason said. “And we set up a bunch of different technology working groups that are really about taking the friction out of the system.”

Evvy CEO and co-founder Priyanka Jain spoke with Fierce Healthcare Monday about research gaps in women’s health and how her company looks to bridge them through vaginal microbiome testing.

Jain said women were excluded from medical research from 1977 to 1993 after a drug being prescribed off-label for morning sickness was causing birth defects, adding the ramifications ar still being seen today.

“Women to this day are diagnosed on average four years later than men across over 700 diseases,” Jain said. “And it's hard to not point right back to the fact that we didn't study women until 1993.”

To bridge these gaps, Evvy offers an at-home vaginal health test with clinician-reviewed results and personalized treatment plans. “If we've essentially never studied women, then there must be so many biomarkers in the female body that we under leverage in our definition of health and disease, and so that's our focus,” Jain said.

Jain added Evvy uses AI and precision medicine to “actually predict the right treatment programs” for each patient using the biomarkers.

And, Jain said women’s health needs attention, awareness and funding when asked about recent Trump administration initiatives to focus on women’s health.

“I’m really excited to see the attention and awareness that has been happening,” Jain said. “But now we need to actually move dollars.”

Department of Health and Human Services Chief Counselor Chris Klomp said the administration is focused on bringing in top tech talent as it looks to make the massive, but aging, government insurance system work better.

Klomp spoke on a panel Monday morning at HLTH, where he discussed the challenges in harvesting the data necessary to transform Medicare, Medicaid and other key government programs. Klomp was recently nominated to serve as Deputy Secretary at HHS and is a rising star in the White House.

He said that technology can play a critical role in accelerate processes that have been historically inefficient and time consuming. At the Food and Drug Administration, for example, tech is hastening the process of developing drugs and making approvals, a timeline that previously taken a decade or more.

But embracing technology in this way isn't compromising safety for these medications, Klomp said.

In addition, he said the administration is leaning on the personal nature of healthcare to bring in workers with the tech know-how necessary to drive critical advancements and change.

"Most people don't care about healthcare unless you work in it," he said. "People also start to care about healthcare when you lose your health, or someone you love loses their health. And than it quickly becomes the most important thing to you."

"We're using that as an opportunity to drive requirement, drive amazing talent," Klomp said.

Houston Methodist announced Monday it has expanded its advanced inpatient monitoring care to include rural hospitals throughout Kansas.

Participating hospitals will provide patients with Medtronic’s BioButton, which continuously monitors vital signs, while the Houston Methodist remote monitoring team will review the data and work with bedside nurses.

The vital monitoring devices are used at all eight acute-care hospitals in the Houston Methodist system, across more than 2,500 inpatient beds, according to the Nov. 11 announcement.

“Innovation is most meaningful when we identify patient needs, take what works or doesn't work and find new ways to extend the positive impact,” said Sara Loewy, Houston Methodist virtual care vice president, in a statement. “What we’ve built in Houston has the potential to reach much further. By thoughtfully extending this model into new care settings, our goal with this program is to demonstrate how our system’s existing technology and clinical expertise can strengthen access and improve outcomes in rural communities.”

Loewy added the expansion is an opportunity to “explore how the capabilities of a major health system can be shared across geographic boundaries.”

While 72% of health tech startups lead with “AI-powered” in their descriptors, zero surveyed venture capitalists in a new report from HLTH and SolComms said the phrase increased their confidence.

Independently surveyed health tech reporters also ranked “AI-powered” as one of the most overused phrases in pitching–in addition to “revolutionizing/transforming” and “disrupting.”

Alongside these survey responses, researchers compared–and scored–the messaging of 72 U.S.-based, venture-backed health tech startups at series A to series C for the “Healthtech Attention Economy Report.” Startups’ messaging across their website and social media was scored on four main dimensions: clarity, differentiation, proof and policy awareness.

SolComms Vice President of HealthTech Isabella Morreale said in a statement the companies that will get attention within the next year “are leading with proof, not adjectives.”

“That means speaking to clinical data, measurable outcomes, and validation from third parties,” Morreale said. “Founder-led storytelling will also continue to stand out. Among the data, one common through-thread for investor and reporter interest was founders with a real point of view on the industry.”

Morreale continued, “Reporters don't need another company description; they need a source who can help them explain what's happening in healthcare.”

Less than half (42.2%) of patients say communications from healthcare providers “often” or “always” feel relevant to their needs, a new report from Lirio found.

Analysts at the behavioral science and AI-powered behavioral intelligence platform polled 1,500 adults across the U.S. for the survey. While 58% of respondents report communications not consistently feeling relevant to their needs, 55.6% rate overall communication experiences with healthcare organizations as “good” or “excellent.”

When asked why healthcare communications are ignored altogether, respondents report generic or irrelevant content (24.4%), too many similar messages (21.8%) and confusing, jargon-filled messages (18.8%) as top reasons.

Nearly half of respondents (47.9%) report the potential value of more personalized, better-timed messages as an “8, 9 or 10” for how much it could help them make better care decisions and stay engaged.

Lirio Chief Behavioral Officer Amy Bucher, Ph.D., said in a statement patients “are not rejecting healthcare communications outright.”

“They are telling us, in specific and measurable terms, that the system is talking at them instead of to them,” Bucher said. "The instinct in healthcare has long been to solve engagement with more outreach - more emails, more reminders, more portals. This data shows that volume is not the problem. What is missing is relevance — content and timing designed for where a specific patient is in their own health journey, rather than a single message broadcast to an entire population.”

Bucher added the healthcare organizations that close the communication gap will be “the ones that use behavioral data to determine the right message, the right channel, and the right moment for each individual patient, which is the model Lirio was built to deliver."

Community-based specialty palliative care provider Vynca is expanding its reach into four more states.

Patients will now be able to access Vynca’s services in Georgia, Hawaii, New Jersey and Texas. Vynca is one of the first practices approved to provide services under New Jersey’s Community-Based Palliative Care Medicaid benefit, launched in April, according to the Nov. 16 announcement.

Founded in 2013, the company’s hybrid care model combines in-home visits with virtual clinical support and predictive technology, and executives say it has shown 43% fewer emergency department visits and 52% less hospital stays within six months of enrollment.

“Health plan and government program leaders understand the value of community-based palliative care for people with serious illness,” said Darren Schulte, M.D., Vynca CEO, in a statement. “Our expansion in four key states reflects growing momentum to expand specialty outpatient palliative care outside of hospices. The key is to broaden access and convenience for the entire eligible population by offering home-based options. Too often, patients are limited to seeking palliative care when available in the community, at hospital-based clinics and facilities.”

#5770. Scion FR-S, Mercedes-Benz 240D, Suzuki Sidekick: The Dopest Cars I Found For Under $5,000

Friends, I'm going to give you a little peek behind the curtain at how this, your most beloved weekly automotive column, works. It goes like this: I find a bunch of car listings, and then I write a couple thousand words about them. You might expect the former to be the fun part, browsing all week for new and interesting listings, but it's actually the back half I really enjoy. See, finding listings has a problem: Eventually, things get old.

That's why you need gimmicks. Cars from a certain area, cars with a certain theme, cars from history's greatest cinematic achievement. Today, the gimmick is price: A hard cap of $5,000, which no vehicle exceeds. I honestly expected a bunch of beige commuter cars in questionable stated of repair, but I'm shocked at how good the offerings were in rust-free states. We've got Benzes, BMWs, and bikes as far as the eye can see. Welcome, my friends, to a budget-conscious edition of the week's Dopest Cars.

Remember when nice FR-Ses or BRZs cost five figures? Well, they still do. This example is no one's definition of immaculate, but it should be everyone's definition of a deal. This is Miata money! Less than Miata money! For under five grand, you could have one of the best-handling chassis out there, and with an engine that's not even blown! Yet. Probably.

Even if/when that does happen, $5,000 leaves plenty of room in the budget for something new to go under that theoretically carbon hood. K-swap, 2JZ, RB26, LS, EJ257, everything fits. Do whatever you want forever with this car, because it's up for whatever. You can fit anything between those front wheels, and you should. Do something cool with it, then reach out to me and send me pictures and videos of the cool thing you did. I'll write about it. That's an Amber promise. (Amber does not get to make these promises. -Ed)

Not only is there a new liquid-cooled replacement for this old 411cc Himalayan out there, in the form of the Himalayan 450, but there's now a bigger brother in Enfield's adventure lineup with the Himi 750. This is neither of those, but they're still relevant here because their very existence makes the first-generation Himalayan cheaper by comparison. It's slower, less powerful, and altogether not as advanced a bike — perfect for those of you looking to get started with something approachable.

Personally, I see the appeal in a dead-simply little ADV like the Himalayan 411. There's so little to go wrong, it's the kind of adventure bike that you can actually really adventure with. Sure, service intervals aren't Honda long, but good luck getting an Africa Twin for three grand. The Himalayan won't get you anywhere fast, it won't be the most stylish way around, but it'll certainly get you where you're going.

Yeah, I was surprised too. A Z32 300ZX, in seemingly good shape, for under $5,000. Are cars just free in the states where they don't rust away into dust after two winters? Do you Arizonans just have your pick of any cool car you want for approximately the price of a Costco hot dog? Don't tell me. I can't bear to know.

Anyway, this 300ZX isn't perfect, so at least I can take some solace in that while I scroll my locally-available rustbuckets and cry myself to sleep. It needs a whole wheel bearing, something that's surely a pain to replace on a completely rust-free car where none of the undercarriage bolts have fused to each other and become one piece of metal that's inseparable no matter how much heat and torque you apply. Surely that's the case. Please just let me have this one. Not even this car, just this dream of perfect-car availability outside my region.

Pink R6! Well, pinkish gray. It's pinker than any factory fairings for the bike, at least. Actually, none of you are allowed to buy this one, I want it for myself once I win a quick Powerball. Just keep scrolling to the next slide.

Mister Two? More like mister too expensive, except in Southern California where these can apparently be had for $4,500. I see why so many car and bike people live there, with the beautiful roads and temperate climate and availability of cars that aren't just piled of rust with a VIN. I get the appeal, but unfortunately I can never join you all. If I spend more than five days in LA I start to go mad due to lack of walkable infrastructure.

Anyway, MR2. This one's not a turbo car, but that doesn't really matter for this kind of money. It also has a beat-up body kit, but again I don't really care. In fact, I prefer a car that has a couple dents, dings, and battle scars — it wears its story on its body panels. This isn't a garage queen, it's a car that's really been used the way its engineers and designers intended. That's worth celebrating, and each rock scratch and bit of drift stitching is a celebration in itself.

Are people over 240Ds now? Have they all moved on to J80 Land Cruisers or something? Back in my day, a 240D in this kind of condition for this kind of money would barely last a day on Marketplace or Craigslist, let alone the weeks this one's been on the market. I know, it's not a wagon, but still. It's not gasoline either!

The seller of this particular 240 claims that it not only runs and drives, but has a fairly considerable amount of work done under the hood. The battery, starter, glow plugs, injectors, and fluids are all new. There's also some unspecified "work" on the head, which probably doesn't mean it's been overheated and warped at some point in its history. I'd bet that didn't happen. How would you even overheat a dependable old Volvo diesel like that, even if you wanted to? These things are so bulletproof.

Not every sub-$5,000 car on Facebook Marketplace is an enthusiast icon. I accept that. That doesn't mean that the remainder have to be bad, though — they can be beloved commuter cars with more sporting pretensions than they really need, like this Mazda3. It's no MazdaSpeed, sure, but it's a stick-shift compact sedan with Mazda's jinba ittai philosophy behind its chassis, engine, and suspension design. I think that's pretty good.

This one seems to be in good shape, and the seller certainly claims the same, though it's a little tough to tell what exactly is going on in the photos. They're so smudged, or blurry, or streaked with sun — I can't even tell why they're wrong, I just know that they are. It's still a good car, but damn, Marketplace sellers. Step your photography game up. Or, at least, wipe your phone camera on your shirt before you take your listing photos.

There's been a Prelude parked outside my girlfriend's apartment for a few weeks now, and it looks a lot like this one. Red, not white, but in a similar state of aged-yet-solid — not the cleanest, not the stock-est, but still more than drivable. Well, I assume it's drivable, but it hasn't moved for street sweeping in a while. I hope it's drivable.

This Prelude not only drives, but ought to drive pretty well — it's an Si model, after all. The seller says it's "mechanically pristine" but that the interior needs work, though it looks perfect inside and out to my eye. Maybe I just have lower standards for my car interiors, but this one looks great. All I can see is a bit of work heeded on the sunroof shade, and what might be the tiniest rip in the side of the driver's seat. I don't think either of those are worth addressing with anything more than a bit of gaffer's tape, honestly.

Hey, it's my old bike! Not exactly, mine was a better color, but I did ride a G 310 GS when I first moved to New York and started working at the good ship Jalopnik. I maintain that a baby ADV is secretly the best way to get started on two wheels, provided you're tall enough to manage the seat height —  they can do a bit of everything, and they'll help you figure out where you want to spend your two-wheel time. Try it all on a small adventure bike, then see what you like doing best and cater your next bike towards that.

This particular G 310 GS, though, has one benefit over mine: It's much cheaper. I sold mine for something like $6,000, and this one's asking just $4,000 — surely you can talk the seller down from that. Imagine picking this bike up for a cool $3,500! You'd have a fantastic beginner bike. I got almost too comfortable on mine, riding it sidesaddle and one-legged through Brooklyn traffic, and you could get that same level of comfort on two wheels.

C'mon, I don't need to sell you on this one. A Suzuki Sidekick for under $2,000! Just go buy it.

#5769. First siRNA Therapy Approved for Myasthenia Gravis

— Cemdisiran is the second C5 inhibitor the FDA has authorized in a week

The FDA approved subcutaneous cemdisiran (Livsayis), a small interfering RNA (siRNA) therapy, to treat generalized myasthenia gravis in adults who are anti-acetylcholine receptor (AChR) antibody-positive, Regeneron announced Wednesday.

Cemdisiran targets complement component 5 (C5), inhibiting terminal complement activation, a key driver of AChR-positive myasthenia gravis. It is the first approved siRNA therapy for myasthenia gravis.

The drug is the second C5 inhibitor the FDA has authorized to treat myasthenia gravis in a week, following the agency's approval of gefurulimab (Klygefa) last Friday.

The approval of cemdisiran was based on data from the 24-week phase III NIMBLE trial. For the primary outcome, Myasthenia Gravis-Activities of Daily Living (MG-ADL) scores improved from baseline by 4.5 points in the cemdisiran group versus 2.2 points in the placebo group, corresponding to an adjusted improvement of 2.3 points (P=0.0005). MG-ADL improvements were seen as early as 2 weeks after starting treatment.

A key secondary outcome showed a 4.2-point improvement in Quantitative Myasthenia Gravis (QMG) total scores at 24 weeks compared with a 1.5-point improvement with placebo, corresponding to an adjusted improvement of 2.8 points (P=0.0015).

The MG-ADL is a patient-reported measure of disease severity and functional impairment, with scores ranging from 0 to 24. The QMG is a physician-administered evaluation of muscle function, with scores ranging from 0 to 39.

In the NIMBLE trial, adverse events occurred in 69% of participants in the cemdisiran group and 77% in the placebo group. The most common adverse event in the cemdisiran group was upper respiratory tract infection (12%), which occurred at a similar rate in the placebo group (11%).

Serious adverse events were less frequent in the cemdisiran group (3%) than in the placebo group (14%). No serious or meningococcal infections were reported in the cemdisiran group.

No deaths were reported during the double-blind treatment period. Two deaths occurred afterward: one, due to pneumonia, was considered treatment-related by the investigator but not by the sponsor.

Cemdisiran is administered subcutaneously four times a year and is available only through a risk evaluation and mitigation strategy (REMS) program, Regeneron said.

The drug carries a boxed warning for serious and life-threatening infections caused by Neisseria meningitidis. Besides gefurulimab, three other C5 inhibitors have been approved by the FDA for myasthenia gravis: eculizumab (Soliris), ravulizumab (Ultomiris), and zilucoplan (Zilbrysq). All carry a similar warning, and patients are required to comply with recommendations for meningococcal vaccinations.

People with generalized myasthenia gravis "experience profound muscle weakness that can affect how they talk, see, breathe and move, and with it their ability to carry out everyday activities," said Samantha Masterson, president and CEO of the Myasthenia Gravis Foundation of America. "This approval is a positive milestone for the [generalized myasthenia gravis] community, reflecting continued progress on outcomes that matter most to patients."

#5768. Common supplement could help fight psoriasis, scientists discover

A widely available nutritional supplement derived from vitamin B5 may offer a promising new approach to treating psoriasis, according to research from China. Scientists found that pantethine can calm immune cells involved in autoimmune inflammation, preventing psoriasis from developing in mice and improving symptoms in a small human clinical trial.

The findings, published October 27 in the Journal of Experimental Medicine (JEM), reveal an unexpected connection between cholesterol production and the immune system. By interfering with this process, pantethine may help reduce the excessive immune activity responsible for psoriasis and potentially other autoimmune diseases.

How Overactive Immune Cells Contribute to Psoriasis

At the center of the discovery are dendritic cells, specialized immune cells that help organize the body's defenses. These cells act as coordinators, identifying potential threats and directing other immune cells to respond.

Dendritic cells perform this role by capturing foreign substances called antigens and presenting them to T cells, which are immune cells that recognize specific threats. They also release chemical signals that recruit additional immune cells and trigger inflammation.

Although these activities are essential for fighting infections, problems can arise when dendritic cells become excessively active. Instead of helping protect the body, they can contribute to persistent inflammation and autoimmune diseases such as psoriasis.

"Emerging evidence highlights that metabolic pathways and their associated metabolites play vital roles in regulating immune cell function and autoimmune progression," says Wei-Na Zhang, a researcher at the State Key Laboratory of Biomedical Analysis in Beijing. "But therapeutic strategies targeting metabolism in inflammatory diseases remain underexplored."

Zhang led the research alongside Qing Xia, Ai-Ling Li, and Tao Zhou, also from the State Key Laboratory of Biomedical Analysis, and Cheng-Xin Li from The First Medical Center of Chinese PLA General Hospital in Beijing.

Scientists Discover a Hidden Link Between Cholesterol and Psoriasis

The researchers identified unusually high levels of enzymes called Vanins in dendritic cells from people with psoriasis and several other autoimmune diseases. These enzymes help regulate the processing of certain substances involved in cellular metabolism.

When the scientists reduced Vanin levels, dendritic cells became less active and were less capable of stimulating T cells. They also found that a drug designed to inhibit Vanins prevented psoriasis from developing in mice.

Further investigation revealed why these enzymes might play such an important role.

Vanins convert pantethine into vitamin B5, an essential nutrient that cells need to produce energy. Pantethine is already sold as a nutritional supplement and is commonly used to help lower blood cholesterol because it can reduce cholesterol production.

This connection is particularly interesting because cholesterol does more than circulate in the bloodstream. It also influences how immune cells function. Previous research has shown that cholesterol can stimulate dendritic cell activity, while elevated blood cholesterol is a major risk factor for developing psoriasis.

The team discovered that excessive Vanin activity reduces the amount of pantethine available inside dendritic cells. As pantethine levels fall, cholesterol production increases, causing these immune cells to become unusually active.

Restoring pantethine levels interrupted this process. The supplement reduced cholesterol accumulation within dendritic cells and helped suppress the excessive immune activation associated with inflammation.

"We found that pantethine administration effectively alleviated psoriasis in mice, suggesting that insufficient pantethine levels may be the crucial contributor to hyperactivation of dendritic cells and autoimmune inflammation following the up-regulation of Vanins," Zhang says.

Common Supplement Shows Promise in Human Psoriasis Trial

Encouraged by the laboratory and animal findings, the researchers investigated whether pantethine might also benefit people living with psoriasis.

They conducted a small clinical trial involving 24 patients with the condition. All participants received a topical ointment containing calcipotriene/betamethasone, a combination treatment used to control psoriasis symptoms. Calcipotriene is a vitamin D derivative that helps regulate skin cell growth, while betamethasone is a corticosteroid that reduces inflammation.

Half of the participants also took pantethine tablets, allowing researchers to examine whether adding the supplement improved the results of standard treatment.

After 12 weeks, the patients who received pantethine alongside their prescribed ointment showed greater improvement in psoriasis symptoms. The benefits were especially noticeable among participants who had high blood cholesterol levels before treatment.

These findings suggest that pantethine could potentially serve as an additional treatment for psoriasis, particularly in patients whose cholesterol metabolism may be contributing to inflammation.

However, the trial included only 24 people, and the researchers emphasize that larger studies are necessary to confirm the supplement's effectiveness. The human results also do not establish that the same biological mechanism observed in laboratory experiments is responsible for the improvement in patients.

"Our investigator-initiated clinical trial demonstrated encouraging therapeutic efficacy of pantethine as an adjunctive therapy in psoriasis, but these findings should be interpreted as proof-of-concept for clinical feasibility rather than direct mechanistic validation," Zhang says. "Overall, our study uncovers the Vanin-pantethine-cholestrol axis as a key metabolic pathway governing dendritic cell activation and provides a foundation for therapeutic strategies targeting several dendritic cell-mediated autoimmune diseases."

Materials provided by Rockefeller University Press. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Optum Rx rolls out new pharmacy tools aimed at transparency" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Earlier this year, Optum Rx teased the rollout of new pharmacy tools designed to address medication cost and access.

Now, the company is offering a look at how those tools work.

The pharmacy benefit manager said Tuesday that the tools build on Optum's new and more transparent pharmacy model, which the company announced in May and shifts to a fee-based structure. The model moves away from more traditional approaches linked to manufacturer pricing and prescription volume and offers clients a clearly defined fee structure.

The first platform, called Shop MyScript, allows members to compare prices for their medications as well as their options for pharmacies or delivery before the prescription is dispensed. The tool will notify members of potential cost savings shortly after a script is written.

In addition, Shop MyScript embeds in the prescribing workflow, Optum said, so that the member does not have to make comparisons after the fact. If they choose to keep the existing prescription, it will then be sent to the pharmacy.

Optum said that early adopters have averaged $28 in savings through the program.

"People should have clear information about their medication costs and options when they can actually use it, not after a decision has already been made," said Katte Carey, president of Optum Rx, in the announcement. "These tools give people more information earlier in their journey, so they can make choices that work for them and get the support they need along the way."

In addition, the pharmacy benefit manager announced Optum Assistant, a conversational AI guide that helps members complete routine tasks and track down key information. The tool can triage concerns on a range of topics, from questions about medication and benefits to pharmacy experience challenges.

If the AI guide can't address the individual's needs, they can choose to be connected to live support to find a solution. Optum said about 80% of conversations using the tool led to a resolution without needing a live advocate.

The final new launch aims to support cash-pay options, according to the announcement.

Optum Price Wise will offer members a complete cost breakdown, including the price of a drug and any fees. That total, all-in price allows members to fully understand what their options may be and make the choice that works best for them at the pharmacy counter.

The PBM said new tools like these build on Optum's new and more transparent pharmacy model, which the company announced in May and shifts to a fee-based structure. The model moves away from more traditional approaches linked to manufacturer pricing and prescription volume and offers clients a clearly defined fee structure.

#5765. Scientists finally discover why we learn to love bitter coffee

A first taste of black coffee can be surprisingly unpleasant. Its sharp bitterness is the kind of flavor our brains are naturally inclined to avoid. Yet millions of people eventually come to enjoy that same taste, often looking forward to their morning cup. What changes?

Scientists at UC San Francisco may have uncovered an important part of the answer. Their research reveals a little-understood dopamine pathway linking the digestive system and the brain, helping explain how we develop a liking for certain flavors through repeated experience.

Dopamine is a chemical messenger involved in motivation, reward, and learning. Researchers have long known that it helps the brain recognize experiences worth repeating. However, most studies have examined rapid dopamine signals that appear within seconds of encountering something rewarding, such as the sight of a favorite meal.

The new research, published November 4 in Nature, examines a different system. This slower pathway responds to information coming from inside the body, allowing the brain to learn about the benefits of food after it has been consumed.

"We've shown that this slow dopamine system is what drives us to learn to like certain foods over time, and we can see where and how that happens," said Zachary Knight, PhD, professor of Physiology and senior author of the study.

The findings offer a possible explanation for why an initially unpleasant flavor can gradually become enjoyable. Once the brain connects the taste of coffee with caffeine's stimulating effects, Knight explained, "that coffee starts to taste a lot better."

How the Gut Sends Reward Signals to the Brain

Scientists have spent decades investigating dopamine and its influence on behavior. Its familiar, rapidly acting signals help us respond to opportunities for reward. But dopamine also operates on a slower timescale, through a system that has received far less attention.

According to Knight, this slower process largely unfolds outside our conscious awareness.

When food enters the digestive tract, specialized sensors detect nutrients, including sugar and fat. Information about those nutrients travels toward the brain, where it can produce a dopamine response that develops gradually and continues for several minutes.

To investigate this process, Knight worked with James Grove, PhD, who was a graduate student at the time. They introduced nutrients directly into the stomachs of mice while monitoring dopamine activity throughout their brains.

The researchers used either sugar water or a liquid resembling a milkshake. Delivering these substances directly into the stomach allowed them to separate the effects of nutrients from the experience of tasting food.

The results revealed a powerful, prolonged dopamine response in a specific brain region called the anterior basolateral amygdala, or BLA.

The amygdala is involved in emotional processing and learning, including forming associations between experiences and their consequences. Scientists already knew that dopamine was released in this particular region, but its purpose had remained unclear.

"We could see that this dopamine is part of a different system and begin to understand its role," he said.

Scientists Find a Brain Circuit That Changes Food Preferences

Finding the dopamine signal was only the beginning. The researchers next wanted to determine whether it actually influenced how animals learned to prefer different flavors.

They first interrupted the newly identified pathway in mice. The animals continued eating normally, indicating that the disruption did not prevent them from consuming food. However, they lost the ability to learn that an unfamiliar flavor was associated with receiving calories.

The team then conducted the opposite experiment.

After mice tasted a flavor containing no calories, the researchers artificially activated dopamine fibers in the BLA. Remarkably, the animals developed a preference for that flavor even though it provided no nutritional reward.

In effect, stimulating the pathway reproduced the learning signal that nutrients would ordinarily generate.

Together, the experiments showed that this dopamine system plays a critical role in teaching the brain which flavors predict rewarding nutritional effects.

A Surprising Discovery in the Left Side of the Brain

The researchers also looked for evidence that a comparable process occurs in humans. Brain imaging studies conducted by Knight's collaborators revealed a strikingly similar pattern.

Dana Small, PhD, a psychologist at Yale University, revisited data from an earlier positron emission tomography (PET) study involving 13 men. Participants had consumed either a milkshake or a drink without calories.

Her analysis found that dopamine release following nutrient delivery was especially concentrated in the left side of the BLA.

A separate study led by Marc Tittgemeyer, PhD, and his colleagues provided additional evidence. Using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), which measures changes in brain activity associated with blood flow, the researchers examined 38 adults after they consumed glucose, a simple sugar.

They observed increased activity in the same brain region.

One of the most unexpected findings was that the response was not evenly distributed between the brain's two hemispheres.

In both mice and humans, nutrients produced a considerably stronger dopamine response in the left BLA than in the corresponding region on the right.

That imbalance surprised Knight because brain networks responsible for essential functions, such as feeding, are generally expected to work in a relatively symmetrical fashion.

Why the left side plays such a prominent role remains unanswered. Knight's laboratory is now investigating what causes this unusual difference.

Could This Discovery Help Scientists Change Food Cravings?

Identifying the pathway provides researchers with a clearer picture of how the digestive system influences the brain's learned responses to food. It also raises an intriguing possibility: Could scientists eventually use this knowledge to change which foods people find appealing?

One area of interest involves GLP-1 medications, a class of drugs that mimic a hormone naturally released by the gut. These medications can substantially alter appetite and eating behavior.

Knight's team did not investigate GLP-1 drugs in the new study, so it remains unknown whether they influence the dopamine pathway the researchers identified.

Still, Knight suggests that one possible explanation for some of their effects could involve reducing the dopamine signals generated when nutrients reach the digestive system. If that happens, foods might gradually become less rewarding because the brain would receive weaker signals reinforcing their flavors.

For now, this remains a hypothesis rather than a demonstrated effect of the medications.

The broader implications extend beyond hunger and fullness. Many approaches to changing eating behavior focus on reducing appetite or increasing feelings of satisfaction after a meal. The newly mapped pathway suggests that the brain's process of learning food preferences could eventually become another target.

By influencing how the brain connects flavors with their consequences, future treatments might someday help people develop different preferences rather than simply making them feel less hungry.

"By understanding the steps between nutrient detection in the gut and learning in the brain, it might be possible to fine-tune them to subtly change our preferences for different foods," Knight said.

The discovery offers a new perspective on why our tastes can change over time. From learning to enjoy bitter coffee to developing a preference for calorie-rich foods, what we love to eat may depend partly on a quiet conversation between the gut and brain that continues long after the first bite.

The research was supported by the National Institutes of Health (grants R01-DK106399, R01-DK138127, R01-NS116626, and R01-DK145100 and F31-NS120468).

#5764. Doctor's Mass Shooting Stuns Medical Community

— Colleagues never perceived Matt Lambert as a danger to himself or others

Doctors who knew Matt Lambert, MD, the emergency physician at the center of last week's mass shooting in Washington, D.C., were shocked by what happened, and said they never expected him to do something so dire.

Those who had interacted with him described a collegial, friendly person who showed no signs of any distress or any mental health conditions. Physicians spoke with MedPage Today about Lambert on the condition of anonymity.

One said Lambert spoke about problems with his condo unit, but it was "no different than if I said I was frustrated with a building problem. There was never any dark humor or anything that seemed off."

Nor did Lambert ever talk about guns, they said -- despite the fact he had at least three of them in his apartment the day of the shootings. On Nov. 12, he killed the building's property manager, then shot and wounded four other people before killing himself.

Joel Braithwaite, an attorney who represented Lambert, said at a press conference that he had spoken with Lambert not long before the shooting and said he was in "great spirits. ... I'm at a loss for how things took any sort of turn that would have us here today."

Braithwaite described Lambert as a "humanitarian" who helped people with scholarships for medical school. "He was also a great thinker, an author, someone who's very calm and collected."

Michael Brice-Saddler, a reporter for the Washington Sun, spoke with Lambert about a year ago about his ongoing issues with his condo unit. In a video posted with his report, Brice-Saddler said there were "no indications to me that he was dangerous or capable of violence."

"I went back and visited him multiple times," he said. "If I thought my safety was in question, I would have pulled the plug."

Last December, Lambert said this to Brice-Saddler about his ongoing condo unit fight: "It's affected every part of my life -- my sleep, dietary habits. I pride myself on my resilience, and I've been kind of surprised at how much it has been affected."

Brice-Saddler wrote that that Lambert did sometimes use "intense, combative language -- and at one point, his frustration veered into what at the time felt like dark humor." He made a reference to Luigi Mangione, the suspect in the 2024 shooting death of UnitedHealthcare's CEO who is accused of inscribing "delay, deny, depose" on his ammunition. Lambert said those words described the condo association's legal strategy, according to Brice-Saddler's report.

Lambert also posted something similar last month on the X account he created for his unit: "After months of 'Luigi' tactics (delay, deny, defend) by the HOA, we were finally able to submit an independent engineering report into the record," it stated in part.

Brice-Saddler uncovered something else about Lambert in his reporting -- the sad fact that he was raised in Appalachia by a single mother who died of cancer during his first year of medical school at Marshall University in Huntington, West Virginia.

Physicians who knew Lambert told MedPage Today it was unclear if he had a partner.

It's well established that physicians with mental health conditions don't often seek help, which is particularly concerning given that doctors experience elevated rates of burnout, depression, anxiety, and suicide compared with the general population, according to a special communication published last year in JAMA.

Jesse Ehrenfeld, MD, MPH, a past president of the American Medical Association and a co-author of that communication, said that much work stands to be done on reducing barriers to mental healthcare for clinicians. That includes expanding confidential care options and removing intrusive questions on licensure questionnaires.

"We need to make that a best practice everywhere instead of just in a handful of states," Ehrenfeld told MedPage Today.

N. Adam Brown, MD, MBA, an emergency physician and healthcare executive who writes about clinician mental health, noted that "having letters behind our names as physicians does not grant us any special privilege of not having an underlying mental health condition," and that the U.S. needs to "take very seriously the health and wellness of clinicians."

"We also need to recognize the role that gun violence plays in our society," Brown told MedPage Today. "We need to take a look at both sides of the coin -- the mental health aspect, as well as the accessibility of guns -- to prevent acts like this in the future."

#5763. Alzheimer’s may have early warning signs outside the brain

Alzheimer's disease is best known for its effects on memory and thinking, but new research suggests that some symptoms may develop in a surprising place: outside the brain.

Scientists at the University of Central Florida (UCF) have discovered that genetic mutations associated with Alzheimer's can interfere with the nerves that control muscle movement, even without involvement from the brain or spinal cord. The findings could help explain why some people with Alzheimer's experience changes in walking, balance, or coordination long before noticeable memory problems emerge.

The discovery raises the possibility that movement difficulties could provide earlier warning signs of the disease and that treatments focused exclusively on the brain may overlook important problems elsewhere in the body.

The research was led by James Hickman, a professor at UCF's Nanoscience Technology Center, and Research Professor Xiufang "Nadine" Guo, working alongside scientists at the healthcare technology company Hesperos. Funded by the National Institutes of Health's National Institute on Aging, the study used laboratory systems built from human cells to investigate how inherited Alzheimer's mutations affect movement. The findings were published in Alzheimer's & Dementia: The Journal of the Alzheimer's Association.

"Motor deficits may be an earlier indication [of Alzheimer's]," Guo says. "If we can detect those changes and intervene earlier, that could help delay the onset of central nervous system symptoms."

Why Alzheimer's Symptoms May Appear Before Memory Loss

Alzheimer's is generally associated with progressive memory loss, confusion, and declining cognitive abilities. However, doctors have also observed that some patients develop physical symptoms, including changes in balance, coordination, and gait (manner of walking), years before clear cognitive difficulties become apparent.

These observations have raised an important question: Are such movement problems simply a consequence of damage occurring in the brain, or could Alzheimer's also interfere directly with nerves elsewhere in the body?

To investigate, the UCF team focused on familial Alzheimer's, a rare inherited form of the disease that typically develops earlier in life (from 40 to 65 years of age) than the more common form.

Their experiments revealed that motor neurons carrying mutations linked to familial Alzheimer's could disrupt the connections responsible for controlling muscles, even when the brain and spinal cord were completely absent from the experimental system.

Motor neurons are specialized nerve cells that transmit signals to muscles, telling them when to contract and produce movement. The new findings suggest that Alzheimer's mutations can interfere with this process directly, rather than affecting movement only through damage to the brain.

"This is the first time it's been demonstrated that deficits in the peripheral nervous system can arise directly from these mutations," Hickman says. "It means drugs that target the brain may not fix problems in the rest of the body."

The peripheral nervous system includes the nerves located outside the brain and spinal cord. These nerves carry signals between the central nervous system and the rest of the body, helping control movement, sensation, and other essential functions.

Guo also points out that preserving the ability to move could have benefits beyond physical health. Regular physical activity is associated with better cognitive well-being, so protecting motor function may also help support brain health.

How a Miniature Human Cell System Revealed the Discovery

To examine the relationship between Alzheimer's mutations and muscle movement, the scientists used an innovative laboratory platform known as "human-on-a-chip" technology.

Developed and manufactured through Hesperos, a company co-founded by Hickman, these miniature systems bring different types of human cells together under controlled conditions. They allow researchers to recreate specific biological functions and observe how diseases interfere with them.

Unlike conventional laboratory experiments that examine isolated cells, these systems can reproduce important interactions between different tissues. They also provide an alternative to animal models, which do not always accurately reflect how human diseases behave.

For this study, the team created a miniature model of the neuromuscular junction, the connection where a motor neuron communicates with a muscle cell.

The model was deliberately designed without a brain or spinal cord. This was a crucial part of the experiment because it allowed the researchers to investigate whether Alzheimer's-related changes could cause movement problems independently of the central nervous system.

The scientists combined healthy muscle cells with motor neurons derived from stem cells that carried genetic mutations associated with familial Alzheimer's disease. Stem cells are cells that can develop into specialized types of cells, making them valuable tools for studying human diseases in the laboratory.

The researchers then examined how effectively the altered nerve cells communicated with otherwise healthy muscle tissue.

The results showed that the Alzheimer's-associated mutations could interfere with normal nerve-to-muscle function. This suggests that at least some movement difficulties linked to the disease may arise directly in the peripheral nervous system rather than being caused entirely by degeneration in the brain.

Why Damaged Nerve Connections Can Affect Walking and Balance

Every voluntary movement depends on successful communication between the nervous system and the muscles.

At the neuromuscular junction, an electrical signal traveling along a motor neuron triggers chemical communication that causes a muscle to contract. This process makes everyday activities possible, from walking and maintaining posture to lifting objects and performing precise movements.

When the connection becomes impaired, muscles may respond less effectively to nerve signals. Depending on the severity and location of the problem, this can contribute to weakness, reduced coordination, and difficulty sustaining physical activity.

To evaluate these effects, the research team measured how consistently nerve signals produced muscle contractions and how long the muscles could continue contracting before becoming fatigued.

These measurements provided a direct assessment of how well the nerve and muscle cells worked together. They also resemble aspects of the functional testing physicians use when examining patients with movement disorders.

"You can't move unless the motor circuit works," Hickman says. "When a doctor taps your knee to check your reflex, they're testing that exact connection."

By demonstrating impaired nerve-to-muscle communication in a system containing no brain or spinal cord, the study provides evidence that mutations linked to familial Alzheimer's can produce effects beyond the central nervous system.

However, the experiments do not establish that these changes necessarily occur before memory loss in patients. Further research will be needed to determine how closely the laboratory findings reflect the progression of Alzheimer's in people, particularly those with the more common forms of the disease.

Could This Discovery Lead to Earlier Alzheimer's Detection?

The findings suggest a potentially important new direction for Alzheimer's research: looking beyond memory and other cognitive symptoms when investigating the disease.

If future studies confirm that changes in motor function are detectable early in certain patients, tests of walking, coordination, or nerve-to-muscle activity might eventually help identify disease-related changes before more obvious neurological symptoms develop.

The results also raise questions about treatment. Many Alzheimer's therapies are designed to address processes occurring in the brain, but medications that target the central nervous system may not necessarily correct abnormalities affecting peripheral nerves and muscles.

Understanding these separate effects could help researchers investigate treatments that protect physical function alongside cognitive health.

Human-on-a-Chip Technology Could Transform Disease Research

Beyond the implications for Alzheimer's, the researchers see considerable potential in using human-on-a-chip systems to investigate other diseases and evaluate possible treatments.

Because these platforms contain human cells and reproduce measurable biological activities, they can help scientists observe disease-related changes in conditions that more closely resemble human physiology than some conventional experimental models.

This approach may be particularly useful in drug development, where researchers need to understand not only how a potential treatment affects individual cells but also how it influences interactions between different tissues.

Such systems can also uncover biological effects that may be difficult to detect in animal experiments, potentially helping researchers identify promising therapies and recognize limitations earlier in development.

For Hickman, the progress represents the culmination of three decades of work devoted to understanding disease through more realistic laboratory models.

"These systems let us study disease in a way that's closer to what actually happens in the human body, and that's what we need to develop better treatments," he says.

#5762. Medicare Shared Savings Program saved $2.5B last year: CMS

Medicare Shared Savings Program saved $2.5B last year: CMS" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The Medicare Shared Savings Program has reached the highest savings number in its history, according to new federal data.

The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services said Tuesday that the program generated more than $2.5 billion in net savings for Medicare in 2025, making for the ninth year in a row that it led to cost savings. The agency added that every accountable care organization met or exceeded quality reporting requirements.

ACOs participating in MSSP earned $4.9 billion in shared savings payments during 2025, CMS said, with 80% of organizations earning performance payments.

As of 2026, 511 ACOs representing more than 700,000 providers are participating in the Medicare Shared Savings Program, which represents 12.6 million people enrolled in traditional Medicare, another record.

"Patients want doctors who work together, care that puts their needs first, and fewer unnecessary hurdles—that is what accountable care is designed to deliver," said CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz, M.D., in the announcement. "These record savings show the power of rewarding providers for quality and coordination. We want more people with Medicare, and more of the providers who care for them, to benefit from this approach."

CMS said that it wants to make it easier for providers to participate in MSSP if they choose, especially given the program's results to date. It included changes in the latest Physician Fee Schedule to encourage participation, including increased opportunity for certain ACOs to earn shared savings and new financial incentives to draw in first-time participants.

In addition, CMS said that would create more predictable spending targets that make planning and participation straightforward. The agency is also aiming to streamline patient notices and simplify required technology.

“We are excited to see continued progress on both savings and enrollment for Medicare beneficiaries. Beneficiaries are best served when a provider is watching out for them and coordinating their care,” said Center for Medicare Director John Brooks in the announcement.

Emily Brower, CEO of the National Association of ACOs, said in a statement that the 2025 results "build on years of progress and underscore what the accountable care community can accomplish through collaboration, innovation and the widespread adoption of proven best practices."

"NAACOS looks forward to partnering with CMS to build on this momentum," said Brower. "Policies that unleash innovation, reduce burden, and create sustainability through fair and predictable budgets will allow ACOs to deliver even greater value for patients and the Medicare program."

#5761. Prostate Cancer Screening Is Changing. Health Systems Must Catch Up.

— Better preventive tools should be accompanied by accessible and affordable follow-up

For years, the medical community has been divided on prostate cancer screening. Urology organizations have continued to recommend prostate-specific antigen (PSA) testing, while other societies and groups moved to emphasize shared decision-making and individual choice, after careful consideration of potential risks and benefits.

The American Cancer Society's (ACS) new recommendations incorporate updated data and make a clearer suggestion in favor of screening. Longer follow-up research has confirmed that screening prevents prostate cancer deaths, and advances in diagnosis and treatment reduce complications.

To support that recommendation, we must make the safer approach available wherever men receive care.

ACS now recommends a PSA blood test every 2 years for average-risk men ages 50 through 69, and annually beginning at 45 for Black men and men with a strong family history. Decisions at 70 through 74 should be individualized. Informed patient agreement remains essential, and screening recommendations generally stop at 75 or when life expectancy is under 10 years.

The strongest evidence for this change comes from the European randomized screening trial. After 23 years, men invited to repeated PSA screening had a 13% lower risk of dying from prostate cancer. The absolute reduction was 0.22 percentage points: approximately two fewer deaths per 1,000 men invited. One death was prevented for every 456 men invited to screening. That benefit is meaningful, but modest.

Screening also finds cancers that would never threaten a man's life. Reasonable experts weigh those trade-offs differently: the U.K. National Screening Committee recently declined to recommend population screening. Recommendations for earlier screening in Black men also rely substantially on modeling because trials inadequately represent them. Supporting the new recommendations requires that we acknowledge these uncertainties.

What strengthens the case for screening today is our growing ability to separate an elevated PSA from a mandatory biopsy, and a cancer diagnosis from an automatic, potentially debilitating treatment.

An elevated PSA should first be confirmed before further evaluation. MRI can then help determine who needs a biopsy. In the Göteborg-2 randomized trial, an MRI-directed approach reduced detection of clinically insignificant cancers by 57% compared with routine systematic biopsy. That finding supports a more selective diagnostic process, although it does not yet prove equivalent long-term survival.

Biopsy itself can be made safer. Transperineal biopsy reaches the prostate through the skin rather than the rectum (e.g. transrectal biopsy, which is the historically more common approach). In the PREVENT randomized trial, infections occurred in none of the men receiving this approach without preventive antibiotics, compared with 1.6% undergoing transrectal biopsy with targeted antibiotics. Cancer detection was similar.

For appropriately selected low-risk cancers, active surveillance can spare or postpone treatment. In the prospective Canary PASS study, estimated prostate cancer mortality at 10 years was 0.1%, and metastasis occurred in 1.4%. About half had received treatment by then. Surveillance means scheduled reassessment and intervention when warranted; its safety depends on continued and adequate follow-up.

Treatment is improving too. In the randomized MIRAGE trial, MRI-guided radiation with smaller treatment margins reduced cumulative moderate-or-worse urinary toxicity over 2 years from 51% to 27%, compared with CT-guided treatment. Bowel toxicity also fell. These results support precision in radiation delivery, while longer follow-up remains important.

In surgery for radical prostatectomy, the NeuroSAFE PROOF trial used rapid examination of tissue during the operation to guide nerve preservation. Among men with good erectile function beforehand, the approach improved erectile-function scores 1 year later and early continence recovery. Neither technique eliminates treatment harms, but both show that preserving quality of life can be a measurable treatment objective.

Aligning these advances with a safe screening program requires changes in how we deliver and pay for care.

First, insurers should cover the entire recommended evaluation without financial barriers: repeat PSA testing, appropriate MRI or biomarkers, and biopsy when indicated. A study of privately insured men found that median out-of-pocket spending for MRI plus biopsy reached up to $620 in 2020. A screening recommendation loses value when patients cannot afford the steps needed to interpret its result safely. Making this a nationwide requirement may take an updated U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommendation with an A or B grade, explicit protection for follow-up testing, or legislation. The task force's current C grade does not trigger the Affordable Care Act's no-cost preventive coverage requirement.

Second, health systems need reliable referral pathways. Primary care teams should know where to send patients, who tracks abnormal results, and how quickly evaluation should occur. MRI quality and interpretation require oversight. A negative scan cannot become a reason to abandon follow-up when other findings remain concerning. Regional imaging networks, specialist consultation and patient navigation can help extend expertise beyond major cancer centers.

Third, active surveillance must be supported as ongoing care. Patients need understandable explanations, dependable recall systems, and accessible reassessment. Payment should recognize the clinical work involved in monitoring a cancer carefully. Men also should have access to balanced consultations about surgery and radiation, including likely effects on sexual, urinary, and bowel function.

Finally, health systems need to measure whether screening delivers better outcomes. Quality programs should track unresolved abnormal results, biopsy-related infections, surveillance participation, treatment complications, and diagnoses of metastases. Results should be examined by ethnicity, insurance, and geography to identify gaps and guide improvement. Research programs should also expand enrollment of Black men in screening and surveillance studies, so future recommendations rest on evidence that better represents those at greatest risk.

I support the ACS recommendations. We now have stronger evidence that screening saves lives and better tools to reduce its harms. We need to make those tools available to every man we screen, with affordable follow-up, careful decisions about treatment, and support throughout his care.
