#5728. Opinion: More surgeons in Africa isn’t enough when only 10% are women

We ranked the 25 most valuable publicly traded Chinese drugmakers

Vadset is a research collaborator at Harvard Medical School’s Program in Global Surgery and Social Change and a fourth-year medical student at Albert Einstein College of Medicine.

A voice cuts through the commotion of the Kigali operating room — calm and resolute, directing the staff as they prep the patient. Standing at the head of the table is Dr. Françoise Mukagaju, the first female plastic surgeon in Rwanda. Beside her is Dr. Victoire Mukamitari, the soon-to-be second.

I watched this film from a theater in New York, half a world away, during the 81st United Nations General Assembly, a week filled with speeches about human capital and health systems built to last. “The Making of a Surgeon” follows Mukamitari through the operating room, as well as her training, her family, and the expectations of both. I saw what the week’s speeches kept missing: Global surgery cannot grow its workforce without women, yet the systems built to grow it are not required to measure them.

A recent analysis of the surgeon workforce in 12 of the 14 member countries of the College of Surgeons of East, Central and Southern Africa (COSECSA) found that women make up one-tenth of the surgical workforce. This number has gone unchanged since 2015 despite a 42% increase in the total number of surgeons in the region. Meanwhile, 5 billion people worldwide lack access to safe and affordable surgical care.

I was 15 when a friend’s mother told me I would never be a surgeon. Fortunately, I live where many female surgeons have paved the way for hopeful women and young girls — a luxury many across the globe do not have. (In the U.S., about 30% of surgeons are female.) One international study of women surgeons found that 56.4% had been told they could not be a surgeon because of their gender.

When the film’s moderator asked Mukagaju how she earned the respect of her male colleagues, her answer was simple: be excellent, and the respect will follow. Excellence is worth striving for. But that answer carries a quiet condition: that a woman must first prove herself exceptional before she is afforded the same respect and opportunity as her male colleagues. More importantly, though, excellence cannot be demonstrated without opportunity. Before a woman can prove that she belongs at the table, someone has to consider her, so perhaps the question is not simply, “How can women earn a seat at the table?” but rather, “How do we make sure women are given the opportunity to take one?”

But you cannot widen the door you refuse to measure. When the Lancet Commission on Global Surgery set its six global indicators for measuring surgical systems, specialist surgeon, anesthesiologist, and obstetrician density was defined, but with no breakdown by sex. A gap that goes unmeasured cannot be fixed, and what can’t be fixed won’t be funded. The vehicle to resolve this already exists: National Surgical, Obstetric, and Anesthesia Plans (NSOAPs), which serve in part as the platforms whose data drives funding decisions. Writing gender-disaggregated indicators into NSOAPs can bring visibility to this disparity. The method itself is not missing — only the decision to look.

Some will argue that gender equity in surgery is a soft target, and that the real crisis is the sheer shortage of surgeons. They’re half right: The shortage is the crisis. That same 42% growth in surgeons raised density by just 0.06 surgeons per 100,000 people. At that pace, the region will not train its way out of this gap by recruiting from the same narrow pool.

Women comprise roughly 40% of recent medical graduates in sub-Saharan Africa, yet they remain that same one-tenth of its surgeons because of barriers along the pipeline. Research suggests they’re discouraged from choosing surgery in medical school, harassed during residency, and face gendered assumptions and family pressures once they’re in practice. The low percentage of women among surgeons is not an aside to the workforce shortage. It is one of its causes. You cannot close the surgical gap while drawing surgeons almost entirely from the same narrow pool of men in each graduating class: mostly men.

The will is not absent. The Pan African Women’s Association of Surgeons connects women surgeons across the continent for mentorship, and regional colleges like COSECSA, among others, run their own initiatives. But mentorship networks and good intentions alone will not garner the money while the gap they address remains invisible in national plans.

Uplifting women in global surgery belongs in every one of these conversations, from NSOAPs to residency programs to the U.N. General Assembly. It is not the sole answer to a 5-billion-patient crisis. But it is a lever we can measure, fund, and act on now — and a promise to the women and girls who are still being told this work is not for them. More women standing at the operating table, like Mukagaju and Mukamitari, is how health systems are built to last.

Taylor Vadset is a research collaborator at Harvard Medical School’s Program in Global Surgery and Social Change and a fourth-year medical student at Albert Einstein College of Medicine.

#5727. Study of 750,000 pregnancies reveals a surprising twist about Ozempic and Wegovy

A major study involving more than 750,000 pregnancies has uncovered an important difference in the potential pregnancy risks of popular weight loss medications such as Ozempic and Wegovy. Women who unintentionally used these drugs shortly before or during early pregnancy were more likely to give birth prematurely, but only when the medications had been prescribed to treat existing diabetes.

Among women taking the same medications for weight management, researchers found no significant association with premature birth or other pregnancy complications examined in the study.

The findings suggest that diabetes itself, rather than the medications, may be responsible for the increased risk of early delivery. The research was published in Human Reproduction Open, a leading journal in reproductive medicine.

The medications examined included semaglutide (brand names: Ozempic, Wegovy) and liraglutide (Saxenda). Both belong to a widely used group of drugs known as GLP-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs). Originally developed to manage type 2 diabetes, these medications also suppress appetite, making them effective treatments for weight loss. However, their safety during pregnancy has not been established.

Why Ozempic and Similar Drugs Raise Pregnancy Concerns

Professor Henriette Svarre Nielsen, who led the research at the Department of Gynecology and Obstetrics at Copenhagen University Hospital Hvidovre in Hvidovre, Denmark, explained that the rapid rise in GLP-1 prescriptions has created an urgent need for better information about pregnancy exposure.

"GLP-1 RA treatment has, within the last few years, become the medication with the sharpest increase in prescriptions worldwide. Current guidance suggests the treatment should be stopped eight weeks prior to planning a pregnancy. However, this is based on early-phase model organism studies, and not real-world evidence. Nonetheless, because of its widespread adoption, inadvertent exposure in early pregnancy is inevitable, and there is hardly any evidence to guide clinical counseling when it happens."

To investigate these concerns, researchers examined whether accidental exposure to GLP-1 medications around conception was associated with complications during pregnancy. They focused on preterm birth (birth before 37 weeks), pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes, delivering a baby that was unusually large for its gestational age, stillbirth, and placental problems.

Study Examines More Than 750,000 Pregnancies

The research team used Denmark's nationwide health registries to examine 756,636 pregnancies involving a single baby among 480,231 women. All pregnancies resulted in deliveries between October 1, 2009, and December 31, 2023.

The researchers classified a pregnancy as having possible accidental exposure to GLP-1 medications if the woman filled a prescription for semaglutide or liraglutide during the eight weeks before or after the first day of her last menstrual period.

This 16-week period included the time when a woman might not yet realize she was pregnant, as well as the early stages of fetal development when major organs begin to form.

Of the pregnancies included in the study, 529 involved prescription records indicating exposure to GLP-1 medications during this period.

To make the comparisons more reliable, the researchers accounted for several characteristics that could influence pregnancy outcomes. These included maternal age, body mass index (BMI), smoking habits, location, education, and whether the woman already had diabetes. They also considered the month and year of pregnancy to account for possible seasonal patterns and changes over time.

Diabetes May Be the Key to Premature Birth Risk

The results revealed a striking distinction between women prescribed GLP-1 drugs for diabetes and those using them for weight loss.

Dr. Kathrine Hviid, the study's first author and a PhD student in the same department, said the findings could help shape future research and improve medical guidance for women who unknowingly use these drugs during early pregnancy.

"We made some extremely important findings that have implications for future studies, such as randomized controlled trials of GLP-1 RA usage in pregnancy, and for clinical counseling.

"We found that these medications were associated with an increased risk of preterm birth, but the risk was only present when the medication was used for diabetes treatment, and not for weight management. This suggests that the underlying condition of diabetes, rather than the medication, may be driving this association."

At first, women with GLP-1 prescriptions appeared to experience several pregnancy complications more frequently than those without exposure. However, most of these associations were no longer statistically significant once the researchers accounted for other factors that could affect pregnancy outcomes.

The remaining significant association involved premature birth among women who had been prescribed liraglutide or semaglutide to manage diabetes.

Compared with women who had not been exposed to these medications, the adjusted odds of premature delivery were 70% higher among women taking liraglutide for diabetes and 84% higher among those taking semaglutide for diabetes.

The researchers' accompanying announcement also reported estimated increases of approximately 11% for semaglutide and 9% for liraglutide among women with pre-existing diabetes.

Crucially, the same elevated risk of premature birth was not observed when the medications were prescribed specifically for weight management.

This difference suggests that the underlying medical condition may play a larger role in pregnancy outcomes than exposure to the medications themselves.

What the Findings Mean for Women Taking GLP-1 Drugs

According to Professor Nielsen, future investigations must distinguish between women taking GLP-1 medications for diabetes and those using them for weight control. Combining these groups could obscure important differences in their underlying health and pregnancy risks.

"Future studies must take account of the reason a woman has been prescribed these medications, as the risks differ between women using GLP-1 RAs for diabetes versus weight management. This is one of the first studies to examine GLP-1 RA exposure in early pregnancy according to the reason for prescription. As more evidence accumulates, these findings will guide clinical counseling for women inadvertently exposed to GLP-1 RAs in early pregnancy. In Denmark, about 70% of people who use weight loss medications are women and so it is inevitable that some may take it without realizing they are pregnant."

Although the results provide useful new information, Nielsen emphasized that additional research is necessary before changing existing medical recommendations.

In particular, the findings do not justify abandoning current guidance to discontinue GLP-1 medications before a planned pregnancy. They also do not provide enough evidence to establish new clinical counseling recommendations based on why the drugs were prescribed.

Important Limitations of the Pregnancy Study

One of the investigation's greatest strengths was its size, with health records covering more than three-quarters of a million pregnancies.

However, the study was observational, meaning it could identify associations but could not determine whether GLP-1 medications directly caused premature births. Other factors, including the effects of diabetes itself, may help explain the results.

Another limitation was that the researchers relied on prescription records. Although they could determine whether a woman had filled a prescription, they could not confirm whether she had actually taken the medication.

The researchers nevertheless believe that most women who purchased the drugs were likely to have used them because of their substantial cost.

In Denmark, patients generally contribute toward the cost of GLP-1 injections, although government subsidies are available for diabetes treatment. For example, a 1mg injection of Wegovy or Ozempic (semaglutide) costs approximately €180 and €114, respectively, with the diabetes subsidy reflected in the lower price.

Dr. Hviid said: "Because of the high cost, we assume that compliance is very high among the women prescribed GLP-1 RAs."

Experts Call for More Individualized Pregnancy Guidance

The findings also attracted attention from researchers outside Denmark.

In an invited commentary published alongside the study, Drs. Yeyi Zhu and Monique Hedderson of Kaiser Permanente Northern California and the Center for Upstream Prevention of Adiposity and Diabetes Mellitus in Pleasanton, California, described the results as important additions to the growing research on GLP-1 medications and reproductive health.

They wrote that the findings "complement and extend an emerging evidence base on the reproductive safety of GLP-1 RAs."

The researchers also emphasized that the distinction between diabetes treatment and weight management could help doctors provide more personalized advice to women who accidentally used these medications around conception.

"For clinicians, the study by Hviid et al. (2026) may inform preconception and early pregnancy counseling. The observation that elevated preterm birth risk was confined to women treated for diabetes, and not to those using GLP-1 receptor agonists for weight management, supports more balanced, individualized discussions with patients who may have experienced inadvertent periconceptional exposure. For patients with diabetes, the study reinforces the importance of recognizing diabetes as an important risk factor for obstetric complications and prioritizing metabolic health and glycemic management before and during pregnancy."

Ultimately, the study highlights why a woman's underlying health conditions matter when evaluating the potential pregnancy risks of GLP-1 medications. While the findings offer some reassurance regarding accidental exposure among women using these drugs for weight loss, they do not establish that the medications are safe during pregnancy.

Further research will be needed to clarify the risks and determine how best to counsel women who become pregnant while using these increasingly popular treatments.

Materials provided by European Society of Human Reproduction and Embryology. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5726. Aetna unveils new program aimed at offering end-to-end support for moms and babies

Aetna unveils new program aimed at offering end-to-end support for moms and babies" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Aetna is rolling out a new program that aims to provide key end-to-end care for pregnant women, new mothers and infants.

The offering, called Aetna For You and Baby, will be available to all expectant mothers enrolled in an Aetna plan. Through the program, moms will be connected to a prenatal visit in their first trimester and a postpartum visit within 12 weeks of the baby's birth.

Women in the program will also be screened for depression both during and after pregnancy to identify any risks.

In addition to supporting the mother both during pregnancy and postpartum, the program aims to give babies a healthy start by providing at least six well visits through their first 15 months, which offer critical tests and screenings, checkups and vaccinations.

The news of the launch was provided first to Fierce Healthcare.

Katerina Guerraz, Aetna's chief operating officer, told Fierce that maternal care often focuses mostly, if not completely, on labor and delivery, though prenatal and postpartum visits play a critical role in driving positive health outcomes.

In its announcement, Aetna notes that data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention show that about 90% of pregnancy-related deaths could have been prevented, with a lack of access to prenatal care and more complete support making for a key barrier.

"This is a national access issue, a quality issue, and it's an affordability problem," she said.

In addition, it's not uncommon for programs that aim to drive better maternal outcomes to lack services for the babies, who in the first year of life undergo a wide array of critical developmental milestones, Guerraz said.

Aetna, as the third-largest insurer in the U.S., sees about 200,000 deliveries a year among its members. That means the success of this program could have a significant impact in a short amount of time, supporting at least 1 million babies over the next five years, she said.

Aetna for You and Baby also builds on a broader push within the company to build a more personalized and simple experience for members. For instance, the company established a program that embeds Aetna nurses in the hospital to support discharge planning and transitions for members, and Guerraz said that holds potential in the maternal care space.

For example, if a baby needs to stay in the neonatal intensive care unit after birth, having an Aetna nurse in the NICU providing additional support to the clinical team and the member would pay dividends, she said.

Aetna is also plugged into Health 100, a sister subsidiary of its parent company, CVS Health, that offers an AI-powered tool to help patients identify healthcare costs and navigate their benefits, even if they're not members of Aetna or Caremark or CVS Pharmacy customers.

Guerraz said the program is designed to offer something that patients can carry with them if their coverage changes.

She added that the team intends to continue iterating on the program and identifying other barriers to care for moms and their babies.

"This is something that we know is going to have a massive impact," she said.

#5725. Medicare for All Has Capitol Hill Abuzz, but It's Unlikely to Pass Soon, Experts Say

— Instead, gradual additions like lowering the eligibility age are seen as a better bet

The idea of expanding Medicare to cover the entire population -- otherwise known as "Medicare for All" (MFA) or "single-payer" -- has been a popular catch phrase among the incoming Democratic members of Congress.

"In the richest, most powerful country in the world, you should not have to suffer for your healthcare," Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, MD, DPhil (D-Mich.), an MFA supporter, told a roomful of nurses last month, The Guardian reported.

"Medicare for All is at the top of my list," Rep.-elect Peggy Flanagan (D-Minn.) told the Minnesota Women's Press last month.

But is that a realistic possibility, especially when Democrats -- although they gained large numbers of seats in the midterms -- don't have enough votes for a veto-proof Senate majority? Probably not at this point, Katie Keith, JD, MPH, director of the Center for Health Policy and the Law at Georgetown University, in Washington, said in a phone interview. "There is a lot of talk ... that there's a need to improve traditional Medicare before you get to open it up and transition to a single-payer system," she said.

This is best illustrated by Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) -- a long-time champion of single-payer -- who recently came out with a plan to get to MFA, but incrementally. "It doesn't seem to be an abandonment of MFA itself but that's what Sanders came out with -- lowering the Medicare eligibility age; focusing on [adding] dental, vision, and hearing coverage; and covering kids," Keith said. "These are all significant changes."

An incremental approach also appeared in a memo sent in September to House Majority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) -- widely expected to be elected Speaker of the House in the incoming Congress. The memo from the Democrats' Cost-of-Living Healthcare Working Group called for capping Medicare beneficiaries' annual out-of-pocket costs at $5,000 as well as adding dental, vision, and hearing coverage -- all part of the group's "First 100 Hours" plan. Then, during the first year in office, the proposal calls for Democrats to "commit to achieving universal coverage" through "comprehensive examination of various single-payer and public option models."

But aspirations alone won't determine the fate of incoming Democrats' legislation, Keith added. "Who knows what committees these new members will be on? Sure they'll be committed to their campaign pledges, but where will they each be in the Senate or the House to push on policy positions of their choice? If El-Sayed is on the [Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee], that gives him a platform, but he might have other priorities. On the House side, there will be a change in leadership at the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee -- what new members will be joining that? It will be interesting to see who lands where and what their priorities are."

Mark Weller, JD, shareholder at the Polsinelli law firm in Washington, doubts that MFA will make it across the finish line any time soon. "The most ambitious healthcare proposals have little chance of becoming law," he said in an email. "In the Senate, Democrats will have 56 [votes], but it's not 60, and it's certainly not the 67 needed to override a veto. President Trump still has the veto pen, and Republicans can still block things in the Senate."

In addition, "there are competing factions in the Democratic caucus," he said. "The challenge is for Democrats to deliver on the affordability mandate. The alternative is spending the next 2 years explaining why divided government prevented them from doing so. If voters feel the economy is not working for them, hearings on Medicare for All aren't going to make their life better. The trick will be to find some opportunities for bipartisan progress."

MFA also has plenty of influential detractors inside and outside of Congress. "MFA is grabbing lots of attention while keeping candidates from discussing much more important issues like our $40 trillion public debt, how to reduce our $2 trillion-per-year federal budget deficits, solvency of Social Security and Medicare, child and elderly poverty, and climate change," Wendell Primus, PhD, visiting fellow at the Brookings Institution's Center on Health Policy, wrote prior to Election Day in an unpublished opinion article, which he shared with MedPage Today. "Let me explain why it should never be enacted."

First of all, compared to the Affordable Care Act (ACA), "MFA is an even more mammoth undertaking because the 10-year cost of $32 trillion is impossible to finance," wrote Primus, who, as the senior health adviser to former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.), was the lead House staffer for getting the ACA passed in 2010. "While the health plan is generous and would provide more coverage than most health plans today, there will be many employers and individual voters who would consider themselves losers when they compare their tax bill to their out-of-pocket health costs. Those who lose because of MFA will stand in the way of enactment."

"In addition, many key stakeholders will balk at the initiatives to lower healthcare costs that will necessarily result," he added. "Specifically, it will be extremely difficult to get hospitals, doctors, insurance companies, and all other care providers to be convinced that MFA would be better than the status quo. And the fear of the unknown will also be a powerful force against enactment."

#5724. Opinion: More doctors should prescribe exercise after a concussion

We ranked the 25 most valuable publicly traded Chinese drugmakers

Hamilton is founder of the Brain Care Catalyst Foundation.

Two decades ago, a Vespa accident put me in a coma. By the time I came home from acute rehab, I had lost 25 pounds, most of it muscle, and my left side did not work as it should. After months of hospital sponge baths, soaking in a warm bath until my fingers wrinkled was blissful — and then it was time to get out.

I couldn’t. At 40, I did not have the upper body strength to lift myself from the tub; I had to shout for my wife to help. The humiliation was clarifying. I needed a way back, and what I found was exercise.

It began gently, with an Ashtanga yoga instructor who came to the house a few times a week. At first even the warrior pose was a struggle, but week after week, the two sides of my body relearned how to work together, and before long, I could get out of the bathtub on my own.

Later, I traded downhill skiing for skate skiing, the technique biathletes use. With my lingering balance problems, I fell a dozen times or more in every lesson. But once I got the hang of it, the sport was exhilarating and punishing: thighs burning, heart rate high for an hour or more on the trails. One day I told my instructor, Jack Bellorado, a rugged former wilderness guide, that I’d had a great ski and only fallen three times. He looked at me and said, “You must not have been pushing yourself hard enough.”

Nearly everyone caring for me after the accident had been trying, sensibly, to keep me safe. Jack expected something hard of me. I needed both, and medical care for the millions of Americans who suffer challenging concussion symptoms months after their injury is still much better at the first than the second.

For years, the standard advice after a concussion was to rest in a dark room until symptoms passed. Newer research is moving away from that recommendation. In a 2019 randomized trial led by John Leddy at the University at Buffalo, 103 adolescents with sport-related concussions were divided into two groups. One was prescribed aerobic exercise and recovered in a median of 13 days, compared with 17 for those in the other group, who only stretched. In a small 2024 trial, people who had lived with moderate to severe brain injuries for six months or more walked farther and faster after a block of high-intensity training than after conventional rehabilitation. This small but important study needs to be replicated in larger trials and include people with concussions.

Medicine has learned of unhealthy overprotectiveness before. In the early 1950s, heart attack patients were kept flat in bed for weeks, because exertion was thought dangerous. Cardiologists Samuel Levine and Bernard Lown questioned whether prolonged bed rest was helping patients or harming them, and, over strong opposition, got them sitting up in armchairs. Their 1952 paper in JAMA helped start a long shift. Today, supervised exercise is a standard, reimbursed part of recovery after a heart attack. And cardiac care was not alone: over the past few decades, surgeons have moved from keeping patients flat for days to walking them within hours.

Brain injury has been slower to make this turn, in part because Hippocratic caution can turn into overprotection. To many medical professionals, it may seem risky to prescribe exercise. For patients, the injured organ is the one you think with, so trying to do as little as possible can seem wise. Exertion can briefly worsen headache, dizziness, and fog, which can feel like movement is doing harm. There is a grain of truth in the caution: The brain does much of its repair during sleep, so sleeping has a central place in recovery. But adequate sleep and daytime stillness are not the same thing, and the lesson from most other fields is that movement and rest are partners, not rivals.

Exercise may help the injured brain in three ways. The first is better sleep. Sleep problems are among the most common and stubborn complaints after brain injury, and exercise is associated with improved sleep. The second is that exercise alleviates depression, another common complication of TBI. The third is more speculative. Working muscles release lactate, far more of it during hard effort, and lactate can cross into the brain, where studies, mostly in animals, suggest it may help trigger production of brain-derived neurotrophic factor, or BDNF, often called fertilizer for the brain. If sleep is when the brain does most of its repair work, a day’s exertion might help twice over: a better night’s rest, and more for the brain to work with during sleep. However likely, that remains unproven but worth testing.

Today I work with the TBI Post-Acute Care Clinic Collaborative. In conversations with clinicians, I repeatedly hear that exercise is rarely encouraged in brain-injury care and even less often formally prescribed. Patients may leave appointments with medications, referrals, and advice to stay active, but without an exercise prescription.

The evidence has limits. Results from adolescent athletes with concussion may not hold for adults with more severe injuries like mine, and such studies are scarce. Some people’s symptoms worsen with exertion. That is why care must be individualized, so patients don’t have to guess. Patients who want to use exercise to improve their recovery should have help determining what they can safely do: an assessment, a written plan with an intensity set for them, a path for progressing it, follow-up to adjust it, and supervision when they need it. Doctors can put this evidence into practice now, and insurers should cover clinically appropriate programs, as they do for cardiac or stroke rehabilitation.

In 1972, a pastor named Robert Perske wrote about tension in appropriate risk-taking. Perske, who led an association for people with intellectual disabilities in Omaha, Neb., was convinced that well-meaning overprotection was smothering the people it was meant to help. Decades before the rise of helicopter parenting, he wrote that “there can be such a thing as human dignity in risk” and “there can be a dehumanizing indignity in safety!” What people needed, he argued, was a “fair and prudent share of risk.”

Perske’s point was not that risk is good for its own sake. It was that a life arranged entirely around safety becomes a smaller life. I got out of that bathtub, and eventually onto those skinny skis, because people took care of me and pushed me. More patients recovering from brain injury should leave their appointments with an exercise prescription, with guardrails suited to their condition. The effort is theirs to make. The plan, and the support in following it, are ours to give.

Scott W. Hamilton is founder of the Brain Care Catalyst Foundation.

#5723. 5 Exciting Ways to Invest in Real Estate

When it comes to exploring enticing investment opportunities, real estate often stands out as an excellent solution for making and growing wealth. No matter how the world around us changes, there will always be a demand for property in attractive areas. This has led countless people to diversify their portfolios over the years, buying rental properties, second homes, and even office spaces.

In recent years, as the world has continued to evolve, the marketplace for real estate investors has evolved with it. Today, people no longer need to buy and flip entire properties to make money. There are numerous tips for getting started and ways you can start your journey into the property world, and some options are actually simpler and more affordable than you might expect. Here are some of the best, most interesting ways to invest in real estate, if you want to avoid the traditional buy and flip strategy.

Not all real estate investments have to include purchasing actual bricks and mortar in the physical world. The digital landscape has evolved drastically in recent years, introducing new opportunities for innovative entrepreneurs to make money buying virtual assets. As the concept of the metaverse continues to gain traction, digital real estate is growing increasingly attractive.

With digital real estate, companies purchase a section of the blockchain in a metaverse landscape, where they can build online experiences, or simply store other assets. In 2021, sales on four of the biggest metaverse platforms for real estate reached a whopping $501 million. This indicates learning how to invest in digital real estate could be a worthwhile strategy for any consumer. Not only is it potentially profitable, but the digital real estate also requires less work to manage and maintain than a physical house or property.

Even if you’re not familiar with this form of property-based investing, you probably know the term crowdfunding. Made popular by sites like GoFundMe and Kickstarter, the crowdfunding strategy involves individuals pooling their resources together to fund a product or business. In the real estate world, investors can work together to purchase a property, such as a corporate space, warehouse, or block of flats, reducing the initial cost of a purchase.

The approach allows investors to participate in products that would have been impossible to access in the past because of high capital requirements. Individuals can use this strategy to diversify their portfolios with a variety of different locations and property types. Plus, you’ll earn a passive income through rental profits, and property appreciation.

Another real estate investment strategy gaining increasing attention in recent years is REITs. These are basically investment vehicles responsible for owning and operating income-generating assets, such as rental properties and office blocks. They’re traded on traditional stock exchanges and provide individuals with an opportunity to invest in the market, without directly owning a property or having to manage the investment themselves.

REITs can come with several attractive features, including regular distributions of dividends, and the ability to explore a range of different sectors. You can even use this strategy to spread your portfolio across industrial, residential, and commercial properties. They’re also a highly liquid investment option, making them appealing to beginners.

Finally, one interesting way to invest in real estate, without buying a physical property outright, is to spend some of your money on shares in PropTech startups. PropTech, or Property Technology startups, are companies focused on developing tools and real estate designed to transform the property landscape. They develop things like property management solutions, smart home technology, and virtual reality applications for tours.

If you already have experience in the world of stocks and shares, investing in a PropTech company could be an excellent way to utilize your existing knowledge and diversify your portfolio. It’s also a chance to get your foot in the door with a company that’s actively disrupting the real estate space, and the market as we know it.

Investing in property has become a much more diverse and versatile opportunity for individuals in recent years. No matter how much money you can afford to spend, or where your expertise lies, you can find plenty of ways to expand your portfolio with disruptive real-estate investment strategies.

#5722. Scientists discover a common sugar may help cancer cells break free and spread

A common sugar found in many foods and sweetened drinks may play an unexpected role in helping aggressive ovarian cancer spread. Researchers at The Wistar Institute have discovered that cancer cells surviving chemotherapy can release fructose, which acts as a signal that encourages nearby tumor cells to break free and spread.

The findings, published in Nature Aging, reveal a previously unknown way that cancer cells can continue influencing a tumor even after treatment has stopped them from multiplying. The discovery also raises important questions about whether dietary sugar and commonly prescribed cholesterol medications could affect how cancer progresses.

"Some cancer cells that survive chemotherapy aren't dividing anymore, but they're still biologically active," said Aidan Cole, Ph.D., a postdoctoral fellow in the lab of Katherine Aird, Ph.D., at The Wistar Institute and first author on the study. "Instead, they continue to release molecules that send signals to nearby cells. Our study is among the first to show that a nutrient -- in this case, fructose -- can act as one of those signals."

Why Ovarian Cancer Often Returns After Chemotherapy

Most patients with ovarian cancer receive platinum-based chemotherapy, a treatment that uses drugs containing platinum to damage the DNA of cancer cells and prevent them from reproducing. Although many patients initially respond well, the cancer eventually returns in most cases. It also frequently spreads throughout the abdominal cavity, the space inside the abdomen that contains organs such as the stomach, intestines, and liver.

This spread, known as metastasis, is responsible for approximately 90% of ovarian cancer deaths. Understanding what allows cancer cells to escape from their original location and establish new tumors is therefore a major priority for researchers.

Previous studies have suggested that cancer cells surviving chemotherapy may contribute to recurrence even when they are no longer actively dividing. These surviving cells can continue producing and releasing a mixture of substances that influence the behavior of surrounding cells.

To investigate this process, Cole and his colleagues developed an experiment that separated the surviving cancer cells from the molecules they released. They discovered that these released substances, even without the surviving cells themselves, were enough to significantly increase cancer spread in a preclinical model.

"As far as we know, this is the first time anyone has shown, in a preclinical model rather than just a dish, that it's the molecules these cells release -- not the cells themselves -- that drive the cancer's spread," said Cole.

A Common Sugar Emerges as a Surprising Cancer Signal

The next challenge was identifying which substances were responsible for encouraging cancer cells to spread. The researchers discovered an unexpected culprit: fructose.

Fructose is a naturally occurring sugar found in fruit, honey, and other foods. It is also a component of table sugar and high fructose corn syrup, a sweetener frequently used in soft drinks and processed foods.

The study revealed that cancer cells surviving chemotherapy could produce fructose and release it into their surroundings. Rather than simply serving as an energy source, the sugar acted as a chemical messenger that encouraged neighboring cancer cells to become more capable of spreading.

The researchers also uncovered another concerning possibility. In their preclinical experiments, consuming high amounts of fructose comparable to those found in sugary drinks could promote signals associated with cancer spread even without chemotherapy treatment.

This observation suggests that diet might influence cancer progression through a mechanism scientists had not previously recognized. Fructose consumption is particularly relevant in the United States, where high fructose corn syrup can account for approximately 8% to 20% of daily calorie intake in some individuals.

Unlike many factors that influence cancer risk and progression, dietary fructose intake can be changed. That raises the possibility that nutritional strategies might eventually become part of efforts to limit cancer spread.

However, researchers have not yet tested whether reducing fructose consumption improves outcomes in patients with ovarian cancer. The findings do not establish that eating sugar causes cancer to spread in humans, and additional research is needed before specific dietary recommendations can be made based on this mechanism.

How Fructose Helps Cancer Cells Break Free

To understand how fructose encourages cancer spread, the researchers examined what happens inside cancer cells exposed to the sugar.

They used several advanced methods to investigate the biological changes involved, including a CRISPR screen. This technique allows scientists to systematically examine genes and identify which ones influence a particular cellular process.

The experiments revealed that fructose suppresses cholesterol production in neighboring cancer cells.

Although cholesterol is often discussed in connection with heart disease, it also serves essential functions throughout the body. It is an important component of cell membranes, the thin outer layers that surround cells and help regulate how they interact with their environment.

In this case, cholesterol helps maintain the connections that hold neighboring cells together. These connections act somewhat like biological glue, making it harder for cancer cells to separate from one another.

When fructose reduces cholesterol production, those connections weaken. As a result, cancer cells can detach more easily, potentially allowing them to escape and spread to other locations.

This discovery provides a possible explanation for how a common nutrient can influence one of the most dangerous aspects of cancer.

A Surprising Connection Between Statins and Cancer Spread

The cholesterol finding also led researchers to investigate an unexpected question involving statins, medications widely prescribed to lower cholesterol.

Approximately 39 million people in the United States take statins. These drugs work by reducing the body's production of cholesterol and are commonly used to lower the risk of heart attacks and strokes.

Because fructose appeared to promote cancer spread by suppressing cholesterol production, the research team wanted to know whether statins might produce similar effects.

Their experiments showed that statins alone could weaken the connections between cancer cells, making it easier for them to separate and escape.

The finding raises questions about whether cholesterol-lowering medications could influence the effectiveness of chemotherapy in certain situations. Researchers are now investigating that possibility, but they emphasize that the results have not been demonstrated in patients and are not a reason for anyone to discontinue prescribed statins.

"We haven't tested this effect in patients yet, but it raises questions about combining cholesterol-lowering drugs with chemotherapy, especially since ovarian cancer is most common in postmenopausal women who are often already on statins," said Katherine Aird, Ph.D., professor and co-leader of the Molecular and Cellular Oncogenesis Program in the Ellen and Ronald Caplan Cancer Center at The Wistar Institute, and senior author of the study.

Could Fructose Also Help Other Cancers Spread?

Although the research focused on ovarian cancer, the scientists suspect that the same biological process could occur in other forms of the disease.

Cancers affecting organs within the abdomen and torso can also spread to nearby tissues and organs. If fructose influences the connections between cancer cells in a similar way, the discovery could have implications beyond ovarian cancer.

"We think other cancers that spread within the torso -- pancreatic, colon, liver -- could behave similarly. We can't call it universal yet, but we think the effects are not just limited to ovarian cancer," said Aird.

Aird and Cole have already begun designing additional experiments to determine whether their findings can be reproduced in pancreatic, colon, liver, and other cancers.

The research opens a new avenue for understanding how cancer spreads, particularly after chemotherapy. It also suggests that the relationship between nutrients, cholesterol production, and cancer cell behavior may be more complicated than previously understood.

While the potential implications for diet and medication remain uncertain, identifying fructose as a signal that helps cancer cells break free could eventually point researchers toward new strategies for preventing metastasis and improving cancer treatment.

#5721. Healthcare purchasers must weigh hospital quality alongside their prices, Leapfrog says

Healthcare purchasers must weigh hospital quality alongside their prices, Leapfrog says" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Patient safety watchdog The Leapfrog Group released its latest collection of hospital safety grades hand-in-hand with calls for policymakers and stakeholders to consider, or directly tie patient safety reporting to price transparency.

The twice-yearly release brought top marks for 900 out of a total 2,366 graded hospitals, and the lowest “F” score for just three. There were 774 hospitals that earned a “B” grade, 655 a “C” grade, and 35 a “D” grade.

No grades were assigned to another 447 hospitals, a decision the group made after a judge’s ruling in a lawsuit involving the scores it would assign to facilities that did not voluntarily submit their quality data to Leapfrog’s survey (Leapfrog appealed that decision in September). Leapfrog’s decision not to score these has generally shifted its letter grade distribution upward, and the organization has said it is reviewing a potential methodology change for upcoming gradings to incorporate non-submitting hospitals.

Still, “a record number of hospitals are choosing to publicly report their safety and quality performance, and we applaud them for holding themselves accountable to their patients,” Leapfrog President and CEO Leah Binder said in a statement.

At the state level, Connecticut maintained its claim on the largest portion of hospitals earning an “A” grade (64.3% of its total), followed by Utah, New Jersey and South Carolina. Leapfrog also called out Rhode Island and Maine for jumping up the rankings—from eighteenth to seventh for the former, and from seventeenth to eighth for the latter. No hospitals were given an “A” grade in five states: Iowa, North Dakota, South Dakota, Vermont and Wyoming.

A hospital’s assigned grade is calculated by reviewing recent data on up to 22 patient safety measures, including a 10-part Medicare composite of reported patient safety and adverse events. Safety scores for specific hospitals can be searched on the group’s website.

Leapfrog and Binder, in a news release outlining its latest scores, made the case that its grades and similar independent measures warrant a seat at the table in a transparency conversation primarily focused on hospital costs.

“Progress on price transparency is important, but there’s no good price for bad care,” Binder said. “We are calling on the Trump Administration and Congress to ensure price transparency is integrated with patient safety and quality transparency.”

The group backed its calls by pointing to a recent analysis (PDF) conducted by the Purchaser Business Group on Health (PBGH) that reviewed employer claims, federal price transparency data, and quality and safety measures including Leapfrog’s. It “found little to no correlation between negotiated prices and standardized quality measures,” as hospitals that received high safety grades often charged cheaper prices than those in the same market with lower grades.

Leapfrog and Elizabeth Mitchell, president and CEO of PBGH, said the analysis—currently being expanded for practical usage by healthcare purchasers—is an example of how a more wholistic view of prices and care delivery should be considered when weighing a hospital.

“Employers have an appropriate duty to pay a fair price for high-quality care, and they can’t meet it by looking at price alone,” Mitchell said in the release from Leapfrog. “When we put the data together, some of the most expensive hospitals were not the safest. Our members want to buy high-quality, safe care that is fairly priced. That shouldn’t be too much to ask.”

#5718. Florida court tosses Tampa General Hospital's suit against Eli Lilly over 340B discounts

Florida court tosses Tampa General Hospital's suit against Eli Lilly over 340B discounts" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

A Florida federal court has tossed Tampa General Hospital's lawsuit against Eli Lilly over the 340B drug discount program.

Florida's Middle District court dismissed the case on a motion from the drugmaker on Wednesday. If Tampa General Hospital wants to file an amended complaint, it must do so within 30 days.

The hospital initially sued the pharmaceutical company over a policy it implemented that requires providers to submit claims-level data on pharmacy and medical dispensing if they participate in 340B. Lilly said it would pull back discounts for providers that did not comply with the requirement and has done so for several organizations, drawing ire from the industry.

Tampa General said the decision is "unconscionable and immoral" in the initial complaint, filed in July.

However, the district court argued that Supreme Court precedent holds that organizations like hospitals do not have the private right to sue if they have been charged beyond the threshold, based on a 2011 decision. SCOTUS said that the right to sue was not outlined by Congress, so it is not an avenue available to these organizations.

"The Court made clear that there is simply no private remedy to superintend the pricing and provision of these discounted drugs," per the order.

"To permit this suit would be to encourage piecemeal litigation and defeat the [Supreme] Court’s insistence on maintaining the Congressional plan 'harmoniously and on a uniform, nationwide basis,'" according to the document.

Eli Lilly cheered the decision in a statement.

"Today’s decision is an important step toward a more transparent 340B program," a Lilly spokesperson said. "Lilly’s claims data requirement asks hospitals for basic information—information they already give insurers every day—to prevent unlawful duplicate discounts."

"Decades of HRSA guidance and two federal appeals courts confirm that Lilly can lawfully require this information," the drugmaker said. "More than 3,200 hospitals and clinics already share it with Lilly, and we hope Tampa General Hospital will join them."

Tampa General Hospital has sued Eli Lilly and Company over the drugmaker’s “unconscionable and immoral” rescindment of discounted pricing under the 340B program.

The complaint, filed last week for the U.S. District Court in the Middle District of Florida, is early legal fallout from a policy Lilly implemented earlier this year that requires providers participating in the federal subsidy program to submit claims-level data for all pharmacy and medical dispensations. The company threatened to pull the discounts for those that didn’t comply and made good on its threat for a subset of hospitals last month, sparking outrage among provider groups.

Tampa General, a nearly 1,000-bed disproportionate share hospital, confirmed in the legal complaint that it was among those cut off. It is now spending 25% to 50% more on average for Lilly products, “many of which it must purchase because of Lilly’s status as the market’s only supplier of a given drug product.”

Tampa General’s lawsuit frequently describes Lilly in such terms, framing the drugmaker as holding significant monopoly power and wielding it in violation of the Florida Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act. It also often draws contrast to the 340B program’s intent to support the margins of safety-net hospitals providing care to vulnerable patients, against Lilly’s current status as the largest pharmaceutical company in the world by market cap.

A spokesperson for Lilly, in a statement given to Fierce Healthcare, described the lawsuit as “just another part of the broader hospital campaign to fight transparency and hide the fraud, waste and abuse that plague the 340B program.”

Tampa General asked the court to order an immediate end to Lilly’s policy and to award damages for the higher prices to which the hospital was subjected. It contends Lilly’s alleged failure to comply with 340B pricing requirements and decision to continue marketing its products as 340B-discounted are unfair trade practices under the Florida statute.

“The most valuable pharmaceutical company in the world is engaged in a campaign to transfer dollars earmarked for charitable purposes into its own pocket,” the complaint reads. “The direct and inevitable result of Lilly’s actions is reduced healthcare for poor people. Its actions shock the conscience and are self-evidently unconscionable.”

Tampa General, similar to the hospital associations that have protested Lilly’s policy, contends that the claims data it requires imposes substantial administrative burden on 340B providers. Even “hospitals who have caved to Lilly’s new demands” have effectively had the prices for their covered outpatient drugs increased due to those administrative costs, it wrote in the complaint.

Lilly and other drugmakers who have signaled similar plans have said they need claims data to spot instances in which a drug purchase is improperly granted multiple discounts under overlapping programs. The company has also disputed that the burden of its policy is as substantial as hospitals say.

“The claims data Lilly requires hospitals to share is information they already collect and send to insurers regularly,” the Lilly spokesperson said of the lawsuit’s claims. “Refusing to share that same data with Lilly shows that hospitals are more concerned with hiding rampant abuse in the program than improving its integrity. Lilly will keep working to ensure this program serves vulnerable patients instead of hospitals and their for-profit partners.”

The 340B program has proven to be a magnet for industry and policy conflict, particularly in recent years as its scale has ballooned. The divide is most evident in the ongoing clash over a pilot rebate program that the Trump administration attempted to launch at the top of the year but was forced to restart after the hospital industry’s legal pushback.

340B providers also received a shock this past week when the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services floated a significant reduction in its 340B reimbursement to 33.4% below average sales price in its annual proposed rule on hospital outpatient payments.

#5717. Without this protein, damaged muscle fills with fat and scar tissue

When muscles are injured, the body normally activates specialized stem cells that help rebuild damaged tissue. But scientists have discovered that without one critical protein, this repair system can break down, leaving injured muscles filled with fat and scar tissue instead of healthy muscle.

Researchers at the Perelman School of Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania have identified an unexpected role for a protein called TRF2, which was previously known primarily for protecting chromosomes. Their findings suggest that TRF2 is also essential for maintaining the identity of muscle stem cells, allowing them to continue repairing and regenerating muscle throughout life.

The discovery, published in Science Advances, could provide new directions for muscular dystrophy treatments. It may also help scientists understand important differences between muscle regeneration and cancer, including why skeletal muscle can repair itself so effectively while cancers originating in muscle are relatively uncommon.

"For years, TRF2 has been viewed as a protein whose primary job is protecting the ends of chromosomes from damage or corruption," said senior author Foteini Mourkioti, PhD, an associate professor of Orthopedic Surgery at Penn Medicine. "But rather than simply protecting DNA, TRF2 seems to be key to regenerating muscle throughout life."

A Hidden Protein With an Unexpected Role in Muscle Repair

For years, scientists have studied TRF2 because of its role in safeguarding telomeres, the protective structures found at the ends of chromosomes. Chromosomes carry our genetic information, and telomeres help keep their ends from deteriorating or being mistaken for damaged DNA.

The new research shows that TRF2 has another important responsibility. It helps muscle stem cells retain the genetic instructions that make them muscle stem cells in the first place. Maintaining that identity is essential because these specialized cells serve as the body's reserve supply for repairing injured muscle.

Under normal conditions, muscle stem cells spend much of their time inactive. When an injury occurs, they become active, multiply, and help replace damaged muscle tissue. Some then return to a resting state, preserving a population of stem cells that can respond to future injuries.

Through laboratory experiments, the researchers found that TRF2 levels change as muscle stem cells move between these different stages. The protein's activity rises and falls as the cells transition from dormancy to repair and then replenish themselves, suggesting that TRF2 helps regulate the entire regeneration process.

Without TRF2, Damaged Muscles Accumulate Fat and Scar Tissue

To understand how important TRF2 is, the scientists removed the protein from muscle stem cells in laboratory mice. At first, the animals' muscles appeared normal, suggesting that the loss of TRF2 did not immediately damage existing muscle tissue.

Over time, however, a serious problem emerged. The population of functional muscle stem cells began to decline, leaving the animals increasingly unable to repair damaged muscle.

The researchers initially expected the cells to die, since losing TRF2 can produce that outcome in other tissues. Instead, they discovered something more surprising: the cells remained alive but lost the molecular identity that allowed them to function as muscle stem cells.

In effect, the cells no longer maintained the biological program needed to perform their specialized repair duties.

The consequences became clear when the muscles were injured. Rather than rebuilding healthy muscle, the damaged tissue accumulated fat and scar tissue, a form of tissue replacement that cannot restore normal muscle function.

"This completely changes how we think about TRF2's role in these cells," said Mourkioti. "The loss of identity has severe implications for whether recovery from injury is even possible."

A Potential Breakthrough for Muscular Dystrophy Research

The team also investigated whether TRF2 plays a role in Duchenne muscular dystrophy, a serious inherited disorder that causes progressive muscle weakness and degeneration. The disease interferes with the body's ability to maintain healthy muscles, making effective repair especially important.

Using a mouse model of Duchenne muscular dystrophy, the researchers removed TRF2 from muscle stem cells and observed a dramatic worsening of the disease.

Muscle degeneration progressed much faster, and the affected mice had shorter survival times. These findings indicate that TRF2 plays an important role in preserving the regenerative capacity of muscles already struggling with a serious genetic disease.

The results do not yet establish a new treatment for muscular dystrophy. However, they identify a biological mechanism that researchers may eventually be able to target to help preserve muscle stem cell function and improve tissue repair.

How TRF2 Protects the Identity of Muscle Stem Cells

Further experiments revealed how TRF2 performs this unexpected function.

Although the protein is best known for working at the ends of chromosomes, the researchers found that it also attaches to regulatory regions throughout the genome. These regions help control which genes are active or inactive, determining how cells behave and what specialized functions they perform.

For muscle stem cells, this regulation is particularly important. Their ability to repair muscle depends on maintaining a specific pattern of gene activity that preserves their identity and regenerative potential.

The scientists discovered that many of the DNA regions associated with TRF2 contain unusual structures known as G-quadruplexes. These structures form when sections of DNA rich in the building block guanine fold into distinctive arrangements involving four interacting strands or segments.

G-quadruplexes have attracted considerable scientific interest because they can influence how genes function. They are also being investigated as possible targets for cancer treatments.

The Penn researchers found that TRF2 interacts with these specialized DNA structures to help maintain the genetic program that keeps muscle stem cells functioning properly.

"We found that TRF2 works through these secondary DNA structures to preserve the identity of muscle stem cells and keep them capable of repairing damaged muscle," Mourkioti said. "That was completely unexpected."

What Muscle Regeneration Could Reveal About Cancer

Beyond muscular dystrophy, the discovery may help researchers investigate a longstanding mystery about muscle biology.

Skeletal muscle, the type of muscle that allows the body to move, has an impressive ability to regenerate after injury. Yet cancers that originate in skeletal muscle are relatively rare, even though other tissues with substantial regenerative activity can be more vulnerable to cancer.

This raises an important question: how can muscle maintain such a powerful repair system without frequently developing cancer?

The researchers believe that TRF2's unusual role in muscle stem cells could offer clues. By examining how the protein regulates gene activity in muscle compared with other tissues, scientists may gain a better understanding of the mechanisms that support regeneration while limiting the risk of uncontrolled cell growth.

That distinction matters because cancer develops when cells acquire changes that allow them to grow and divide without the normal biological restraints. Finding ways to strengthen muscle repair without encouraging abnormal growth would be an important goal for future therapies.

Mourkioti and her colleagues are now investigating whether the way muscle stem cells use TRF2 could lead to new treatment strategies for muscular dystrophy. They also hope to determine what this mechanism can reveal about cancer biology in tissues that are more susceptible to the disease.

Although additional research is needed to determine whether these findings can be translated into treatments for people, the discovery reveals an important part of the body's muscle repair system. It also demonstrates that a protein long associated with protecting DNA has a much broader role in keeping muscles capable of healing.

The research was supported by grants from the National Institutes of Health/ National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases (R01 DK123356, R01s CA174904, GM101149, and FDN-143330).

#5716. Patients have little say in how brain implant trials are done. Ian Burkhart wants to change that

We ranked the 25 most valuable publicly traded Chinese drugmakers

Disability in Health Care Reporting Fellow

Rose covers disability and mental health, and she helps write STAT’s daily Morning Rounds newsletter. Confidential tips can be sent to Rose on Signal at rosebroderick.11.

So you’ve been diagnosed with ALS — what now? Maybe you join a clinical trial for a brain implant that could help you do things like move your hand or talk to your loved ones. But can you influence the research as a participant? And what happens to the data collected from your brain when the study ends?

A new report addresses these and other questions, exploring how trials of implanted brain-computer interfaces can better address the interests and concerns of participants, who often join in a last-ditch attempt to improve their communication, mobility, or autonomy.

“These studies can sometimes last years, and it becomes a big part of someone’s life. You want there to be as much agency from the participant as possible,” said Ian Burkhart, who co-founded the coalition, with other participants in early studies of implantable BCI devices, to share patient feedback with developers and researchers. Burkhart said the report emerged out of discussions between him and other study participants, who felt they had very little say in how trials were conducted.

The recommendations arrive as the field moves from a niche, proof-of-concept phase into a humming neurotechnology startup ecosystem with eager investors and multiple clinical trials testing implanted devices’ safety and efficacy. Ethicist Anna Wexler believes that scientists need better policies to ensure participants’ rights and autonomy.

“There is no good solution right now. We talk about potentially mandatory insurance policies, escrows, and institutions committing support, but right now we just don’t actually have solutions,” Wexler, a University of Pennsylvania Perelman School of Medicine professor, said during a panel at a recent brain-computer interface industry conference in New York.

STAT spoke with Burkhart about his own experiences as someone with tetraplegia and as a former BCI user shopping around for his next device. He wants to make sure that during his next trial, he has more clarity around the study’s overall expectations, what he can do with the data generated, and what will happen to his care after he is explanted.

You were implanted in 2014 with a device at Ohio State University that helped you move your arm. What happened when the study ended?

When our study was starting to wind down because of some funding issues, the institutional review board said, “Well, we can just have them have the device taken out, and then if it gets funded again, they can just put another one back in.” Like, that’s great when it’s not you that’s going through experimental brain surgery.

To me, it really just minimized my experience down to something more akin to a lab rat versus being a human. The [IRB and the institution] claim to be supportive of the researchers trying to get additional funding and continue the work. And if they really were, they would have seen that it makes more sense to put a little bit more of a pause on it and wait for funding to come through if possible, instead of doing something as disruptive as having surgery.

Most informed consents right now, they’re more of a one-sided agreement protecting the research team and institution versus protecting what the participants may want. If you don’t agree to something, the alternative is to not participate. And that’s fine when you’re first signing up for a study. It changes once you’ve already been in a study and you’re re-consenting to continue on with the study, especially when there are very limited alternatives for treatment for this patient population.

Yes. And then, you know, you add in the psychological piece of using these devices to restore function after a disability. To my knowledge, everyone that’s used a device has an acquired disability versus being born with their disability. So they have that capability, and then they have their disability, and that capability is taken away from them, and then these devices help restore some of that function, and then it’s taken away again.

If there’s real technical reasons that the device stops working or we’re not able to use this technology anymore, that’s one thing. But if there’s just a well, it’s easier for us to administratively close the study, and we can start it back up again in the future, that doesn’t seem like a valid reason to take away and have someone psychologically experience a little bit of their injury or their disability again.

How does that compare to other BCI users’ experiences?

They have had similar experiences where they don’t really know what the end of the study is going to look like. And as a participant, you can leave at any time, but also the researchers can kick you out of the study at any time, within their rationale.

It’s a little bit of a challenge there when you are doing something as intimate as going into the lab multiple times a week, multiple hours at a time, and it becomes such a big part of your life. For it to just be abruptly stopped can be really challenging. … You know, Nathan Copeland, he’s passed 11 years [with a device] now.

That’s practically a millenium in this fledgling industry. What should long-term care look like for BCI users?

We’re past the proof of concept phase [for these devices]. Is there any support for people to maintain these devices, not in a way that you know we’re forcing a company or institution to keep up a manufacturing line, but can there be decisions made earlier on that will allow, if you need a new battery, you can get a battery from company A, B, or C? Versus it’s only one company that makes the battery, and if that company’s out of business, then you’re done? What kind of support can be available so that you can potentially slowly wind down the trial and not have it be as abrupt?

I knew when I signed up [for my study] that this wasn’t going to be a forever thing. It was only supposed to be up to a year and a half, but it continued, we were able to reconsent and expand on the study, and it became a much larger part of my life than I envisioned. To then have such an abrupt ending is not something that anyone wants to go through.

I only had access to the device when I’m going to the lab. Now that people are using these devices at home and you know out in the wild, it’s a much more significant change when there is that abrupt end.

The report talks a lot about giving participants more access to their neural data. What are you proposing?

If you give the participant full ownership of that data, there should be a mechanism where the main research team can have first crack at that data, but then after, if the participant agrees, it allows them to open that up and let other researchers who may not have the resources to implant an individual and capture all this data to see what they can learn from that as well.

I feel like I would balk at that if I was a researcher or regulator.

It really just depends on what information it is, how much of a kind of delay that someone may get, and how exactly those experiments are structured. If I could have shared some of the raw data from my study, so someone sitting around in their basement trying to come up with different decoding algorithms, I think that’s beneficial for the field. And you know, if the researchers are actually motivated by what’s beneficial for the field versus getting their credit and publishing another paper and moving on, I think they would be open to that.That’s really the goal out of these types of devices to help individuals with disabilities have more independence, autonomy, agency over their lives.

Are a lot of study participants asking to run raw data through decoding algorithms in their basement?

I’ve certainly met a few. Most of the participants were like, “That’s way over my head.” But I think that there are plenty of people who would like to put their neural data into an AI tool and see what they can learn.

My study has been over for six years now. All that data is hopefully still sitting on a server somewhere. I’m sure there’s something that someone with a fresh set of eyes could make sense of, potentially bringing a little bit of value.

I certainly think it would be interesting to see what I can find out about my own data, being able to go into the research lab but then, on my own time, I can sit at home and run some other experiments that might be different. Get as much juice out of it as we can. Make sure it’s worth the squeeze.

#5715. Cigna Group Foundation making $31.5M in grants available to community organizations in 10 states

Cigna Group Foundation making $31.5M in grants available to community organizations in 10 states" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Cigna is making $31.5 million in grant funding available over the next three years to nonprofits in 10 states that are aiming to tackle several key community health priorities.

The company said that funds will be made available through its philanthropic arm, the Cigna Group Foundation, with applications open now through Dec. 18. Cigna said in an announcement that it's looking for organizations tackling youth mental health, veteran wellness and the impact of complex health needs on patients and their caregivers.

Cigna said the program seeks to deepen the company's community health strategy to address critical challenges.

The company first launched a new approach to community health and engagement in 2024, and since then has deployed more than $30 million in funding to 190 nonprofit organizations. Projects backed by these grants have reached at least 321,000 people, Cigna said.

"Over the past several years, we’ve seen the tangible impact we can make when we invest in strong nonprofit partners and come together to help communities achieve better health and vitality," said Melissa Skottegaard, board chair of The Cigna Group Foundation, in the announcement. "We’re building on what’s working, bringing together funding, collaboration and the skills of our employee volunteers to address some of the most pressing health challenges facing communities across the street and around the world."

Cigna will allot $10.5 million to each of the three focus areas under the initiative, per the announcement. Youth mental health, for example, has been a leading topic at the company for some time, and the company said it will also continue to build on its partnership with the Boys and Girls Clubs of America in this area.

In that partnership, Cigna has helped build out trauma-informed care services to 90% of clubs, reaching 11,000 employees. The company said that these efforts have supported 1,600 youths, and that its workforce has contributed more than 2,000 hours to local clubs.

Eligible organizations can apply for two-year, $250,000 grants to support programs in the three categories. The funds will be available to groups in Arizona, Connecticut, Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Missouri, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Tennessee and Texas, per the announcement.

Cigna said its foundation will also continue to support community health through its Health Equity Impact Fund.

"Community organizations can be a powerful source of support for people navigating complex health conditions,” said Matt Perlberg, president of Evernorth Pharmacy & Care Delivery and board member of the Cigna Group Foundation, in the announcement. “By helping patients and caregivers connect with resources and overcome barriers to care, these organizations can provide important support alongside essential medical treatment, helping people navigate their health and care journey.”

#5714. 'Grand Slam' Pancreatic Cancer Drug Shows Promise as First-Line Treatment

— Response rate with daraxonrasib plus chemotherapy was 61% in early-stage trial

The first-in-class RAS inhibitor daraxonrasib (Rasonque) in combination with chemotherapy showed promise as a first-line treatment for patients with metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma (PDAC), according to results from an early-stage trial.

Among 61 patients, the confirmed objective response rate with daraxonrasib plus gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel (Abraxane) was 61% (including 8.2% with a complete response), with a median duration of response of 11.1 months, reported Wungki Park, MD, of Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York City.

Median progression-free survival (PFS) was 12.8 months, with a 12-month PFS rate of 51.7%. The overall survival (OS) rate at 12 months was 76.6%.

"This represents a potentially transformative advance in first-line treatment for patients with metastatic pancreatic cancer, already outpacing the high end for the historical overall survival of 8.5 to 11.1 months with conventional chemotherapy," Park said in a press release.

He presented the findings at the EORTC-NCI-AACR Symposium on Molecular Targets and Cancer Therapeutics in Barcelona, Spain.

"These are very encouraging results in a disease where progress has historically been difficult to achieve," said Shivan Sivakumar, PhD, of the University of Birmingham in England, in comments posted to the Science Media Centre website.

"What is particularly exciting is the potential to move beyond chemotherapy as the mainstay of treatment for pancreatic cancer," he added. "By targeting RAS, a fundamental driver of the vast majority of pancreatic cancers, we may be entering an era where molecularly targeted therapies can meaningfully improve outcomes for patients."

However, the findings should be interpreted "carefully" considering this is a relatively small early-stage study without a randomized control group, Sivakumar cautioned. He suggested that if the findings are confirmed in the phase III RASolute 303 trial, "this could represent one of the most significant advances in the first-line treatment of metastatic pancreatic cancer in recent years."

Daraxonrasib, an oral RAS(ON) multi-selective inhibitor targeting GTP-bound mutant and wild-type RAS, doubled OS and PFS in patients with previously treated metastatic PDAC in the phase III RASolute 302 trial. Based on those results, the FDA in August approved the drug for patients who have received at least one prior systemic therapy or who are ineligible for multi-agent systemic therapy, after giving the green light to an expanded access program earlier in the year.

In his presentation, Park noted that current standard-of-care chemotherapy options for the first-line treatment of metastatic PDAC provide limited benefit, with less than half of patients receiving subsequent second-line therapy, "underscoring the need for more effective first-line treatment options."

The RMC-GI-102 platform study is an ongoing phase I/II multicenter trial of patients with RAS-mutant gastrointestinal tumors. The analysis presented here evaluated daraxonrasib and gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel among patients in the metastatic PDAC cohort.

Patients had a median age of 67, and 59% were men. Just over half (54%) had an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 1, 70% had liver metastases at enrollment, and 57% had stage IV disease at diagnosis.

The patients received 200-mg daraxonrasib, taken orally once a day, plus gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel given by intravenous injection on days 1 and 15 in 28-day cycles.

Grade ≥3 treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs) were observed in 75% of patients, the most common of which were anemia (33%), fatigue (16%), neutrophil count decreases (16%), rash (13%), and diarrhea (11%). Serious TRAEs occurred in 23% of patients.

Dose modifications due to daraxonrasib-related adverse events occurred in 66% of patients (most frequently due to rash), while treatment discontinuation due to daraxonrasib-related adverse events was infrequent, occurring in just 5% of patients.
